This tutorial introduces Genie One, a simplified Databricks interface for business users.

This tutorial walks you through:

- Opening the Genie One interface
- Discovering and searching for assets shared with you
- Viewing an AI/BI dashboard
- Asking natural language questions about dashboard data using Genie

- You must have the **Consumer access**entitlement in your workspace. See What is consumer access?.
- Your workspace administrator must have shared at least one dashboard with you.

If your only entitlement is **Consumer access**, you land on the Genie One home page after signing in.

If you have additional entitlements such as **Workspace access** or **Databricks SQL access**, click  in the upper-right corner of the workspace and select **Genie One**.

Use the Genie One home page to find the assets available to you.

- In the **For you**section, browse recently opened assets, favorites, and items trending in your workspace.
- Click **Dashboards**or**Genie Agents**in the left navigation to see all assets of that type shared with you.
- To search for a specific asset by name, type in the search bar at the top of the page.
- To filter results, click  on the left of the listing page:
- **Type**: Show only dashboards or Genie Agents.
- **Status**: Show only- **Certified**assets or your- **Favorites**.
- **Owner**: Search by the asset owner's user ID.
- **Last modified**: Filter by how recently the asset was updated.

- To mark an asset as a favorite, click the star icon next to the asset's name.

Dashboards display pre-built charts and metrics prepared by your team.

- Click **Dashboards**to open the dashboards listing page.
- Click a dashboard to open it.
- Interact with the visualizations by using filters, hovering over data points, and scrolling through the charts.

While viewing a dashboard, you can ask natural language questions about the data using the built-in **Ask Genie** button.

- From an open dashboard, click **Ask Genie**. A chat window opens on the right side of the dashboard.
- In the chat box, type a question about the data, such as "What were the top 5 products by sales last quarter?"
- Review the answer. Genie returns a table, chart, or summary based on the dashboard data.

Now that you know the basics of Genie One, you can:

- Learn about the full Genie One interface. See Use Genie One.
- Explore AI/BI dashboards. See Dashboards.
- Learn about asking Genie questions from a dashboard. See Genie Agents with dashboards.
- Understand what consumer access includes. See What is consumer access?.

You can browse assets, search for specific dashboards, interact with visualizations, and use the Ask Genie feature to ask questions about dashboard data in plain English.

This article introduces fundamental components you need to understand in order to use Databricks effectively.

In Databricks, a *workspace* is a Databricks deployment in the cloud that functions as an environment for your team to access Databricks assets. Your organization can choose to have either multiple workspaces or just one, depending on its needs.

A Databricks *account* represents a single entity that can include multiple workspaces. Accounts enabled for Unity Catalog can be used to manage users and their access to data centrally across all of the workspaces in the account. Billing and support are also handled at the account level.

Databricks bills based on Databricks units (DBUs), which are units of processing capability per hour based on VM instance type.

See the Databricks on AWS pricing estimator.

This section describes concepts that you need to know when you manage Databricks identities and their access to Databricks assets.

A unique individual who has access to the system. User identities are represented by email addresses. See Manage users.

A service identity for use with jobs, automated tools, and systems such as scripts, apps, and CI/CD platforms. Service principals are represented by an application ID. See Service principals.

A collection of identities. Groups simplify identity management, making it easier to assign access to workspaces, data, and other securable objects. All Databricks identities can be assigned as members of groups. See Groups.

A list of permissions attached to the workspace, cluster, job, table, or experiment. An ACL specifies which users or system processes are granted access to the objects, as well as what operations are allowed on the assets. Each entry in a typical ACL specifies a subject and an operation. See Access control lists.

A personal access token is a string used to authenticate REST API calls, Technology partners connections, and other tools. See Authenticate with Databricks personal access tokens (legacy).

The Databricks UI is a graphical interface for interacting with features, such as workspace folders and their contained objects, data objects, and computational resources.

Genie One is a simplified Databricks interface designed for business users. It provides a single entry point to view AI/BI dashboards, ask data questions, and use Databricks Apps, without navigating technical workspace concepts. See Use Genie One.

The Databricks REST API provides endpoints for modifying or requesting information about Databricks account and workspace objects. See account reference and workspace reference.

The SQL REST API allows you to automate tasks on SQL objects. See SQL API.

The Databricks CLI is hosted on GitHub. The CLI is built on top of the Databricks REST API.

This section describes the tools and logical objects used to organize and govern data on Databricks. See Database objects in Databricks.

Unity Catalog is a unified governance solution for data and AI assets on Databricks that provides centralized access control, auditing, lineage, and data discovery capabilities across Databricks workspaces. See What is Unity Catalog?.

reference_note.title: Databricks Fundamentals: Workspaces, Accounts, Identities, and Governance
reference_note.summary: Databricks is organized around workspaces (cloud environments for teams) and accounts (entities that manage multiple workspaces). You manage access through users, service principals, and groups, with permissions controlled by ACLs. Unity Catalog provides centralized governance across workspaces. Understanding these core concepts is essential before starting any real project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks workspace is a cloud environment where your team accesses Databricks assets like notebooks, clusters, and data. Think of it as a dedicated project space in the cloud.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Your team will work inside a workspace. Organizations can have multiple workspaces for different teams or projects, or just one shared workspace depending on their needs.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks account is a single entity that can contain multiple workspaces. It handles billing, support, and (if enabled) centralized user and data access management across all workspaces.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Your organization's account is the top-level container. If your account has Unity Catalog enabled, you can manage user access and data governance centrally instead of managing each workspace separately.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: DBUs are the units Databricks uses to bill you. You pay based on the processing power (VM instance type) you use per hour.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding DBU billing helps you estimate costs for your project and choose appropriate compute resources.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A user is a unique individual who accesses Databricks, identified by their email address.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When setting up your project, you'll need to manage which users have access to workspaces and data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A service principal is a non-human identity (represented by an application ID) used for automated processes like jobs, scripts, apps, and CI/CD pipelines.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When automating tasks in your project (e.g., scheduled jobs or API calls), you'll use service principals instead of user accounts.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A group is a collection of identities (users and/or service principals). Instead of managing access for each person individually, you assign permissions to groups.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Groups make it easier to manage access at scale. For example, you can create a 'Data Scientists' group and grant it access to specific data once, rather than managing each person separately.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: An ACL is a list of permissions that specifies which users or processes can access an object (workspace, cluster, job, table, experiment) and what operations they can perform.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ACLs control who can do what in your project. You'll use them to secure data and resources.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Unity Catalog is a centralized governance system that provides access control, auditing, data lineage tracking, and data discovery across all workspaces in your account.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If your account has Unity Catalog enabled, you can manage data access and governance from one place instead of managing each workspace separately. This is critical for multi-workspace organizations.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A graphical interface for interacting with Databricks features like workspace folders, data objects, and computational resources.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use the UI when you want to visually navigate workspaces, create notebooks, manage clusters, and explore data.

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use the REST API when you need to automate tasks, integrate Databricks with other systems, or build custom tools.

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use the SQL REST API when you need to programmatically manage or query SQL objects.

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A command-line interface built on top of the Databricks REST API, hosted on GitHub. Allows you to interact with Databricks from the terminal.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use the CLI when you prefer command-line tools or need to automate Databricks tasks in scripts.

important_features_or_tools.name: Personal Access Token
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A string used to authenticate REST API calls, technology partner connections, and other tools. Acts as a credential for programmatic access.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Generate a personal access token when you need to authenticate API calls or connect external tools to Databricks.

practical_workflow.action: Understand your organization's Databricks account structure. Determine if you have one workspace or multiple workspaces.
practical_workflow.reason: This tells you where your project will live and how access is managed.

practical_workflow.action: Check if your account has Unity Catalog enabled. If yes, understand that data governance is centralized across workspaces.
practical_workflow.reason: This affects how you'll manage access to data and who can see what.

practical_workflow.action: Identify which users and service principals need access to your project. Organize them into groups if possible.
practical_workflow.reason: Groups make access management simpler and more maintainable as your project grows.

practical_workflow.action: Set up ACLs to grant appropriate permissions to users, service principals, and groups for workspaces, clusters, jobs, and data.
practical_workflow.reason: ACLs ensure only authorized people can access your project's resources.

practical_workflow.action: Choose how you'll interact with Databricks: UI for manual work, CLI for scripting, or REST API for automation.
practical_workflow.reason: Different tools suit different tasks. The UI is good for exploration; APIs are good for automation.

practical_workflow.action: If you need to automate tasks, generate a personal access token for authentication.
practical_workflow.reason: Tokens allow scripts and external tools to securely authenticate with Databricks.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking a workspace and an account are the same thing.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: An account is the top-level entity that can contain multiple workspaces. A workspace is a single cloud environment. One account can manage many workspaces.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Managing access for each individual user instead of using groups.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use groups to manage access. Groups make it easier to grant permissions to multiple people at once and simplify future changes.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not understanding the difference between users and service principals.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Users are for people; service principals are for automated processes and systems. Use service principals for jobs, scripts, and CI/CD pipelines.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming all workspaces share the same data governance if Unity Catalog is not enabled.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Without Unity Catalog, each workspace manages its own access control independently. Unity Catalog enables centralized governance across workspaces.

project_usage_notes: When starting a real project, first confirm your account structure and whether Unity Catalog is enabled. This determines how you'll manage access and data governance.
Create groups for different roles in your project (e.g., 'Data Engineers', 'Analysts', 'Stakeholders') and assign permissions to groups rather than individuals.
If your project involves automated tasks (scheduled jobs, API integrations), create service principals instead of using user accounts for authentication.
Use the Databricks UI to explore and develop interactively, but use the REST API or CLI to automate repetitive tasks and integrate with other systems.
If your organization has multiple workspaces, check if Unity Catalog is enabled. If yes, use it to manage data access centrally. If no, plan access control for each workspace separately.
Generate personal access tokens only for programmatic access (scripts, APIs, external tools). Never share tokens or commit them to version control.

Catalogs are the highest level container for organizing and isolating data on Databricks. You can share catalogs across workspaces within the same region and account. See What are catalogs in Databricks?.

Schemas, also known as databases, are contained within catalogs and provide a more granular level of organization. They contain database objects and AI assets, such as volumes, tables, functions, and models. See What are schemas in Databricks?.

Tables organize and govern access to structured data. You query tables with Apache Spark SQL and Apache Spark APIs. See Databricks tables.

A view is a read-only object derived from one or more tables and views. Views save queries that are defined against tables. See What is a view?.

Volumes represent a logical volume of storage in a cloud object storage location and organize and govern access to non-tabular data. Databricks recommends using volumes for managing all access to non-tabular data on cloud object storage. See What are Unity Catalog volumes?.

By default, all tables created in Databricks are Delta tables. Delta tables are based on the Delta Lake open source project, a framework for high-performance ACID table storage over cloud object stores. A Delta table stores data as a directory of files on cloud object storage and registers table metadata to the metastore within a catalog and schema.

Unity Catalog provides an account-level metastore that registers metadata about data, AI, and permissions about catalogs, schemas, and tables. See Metastore.

Databricks provides a legacy Hive metastore for customers that have not adopted Unity Catalog. See Hive metastore table access control (legacy).

Catalog Explorer allows you to explore and manage data and AI assets, including schemas (databases), tables, models, volumes (non-tabular data), functions, and registered ML models. You can use it to find data objects and owners, understand data relationships across tables, and manage permissions and sharing. See What is Catalog Explorer?.

Storing and accessing data using DBFS root or DBFS mounts is a deprecated pattern and not recommended by Databricks. Instead, Databricks recommends using Unity Catalog to manage access to all data. See What is Unity Catalog?.

The DBFS root is a storage location available to all users by default. See What is DBFS?.

A set of computation resources and configurations on which you run notebooks and jobs. There are two types of clusters: all-purpose and job. See Compute.

- You create an *all-purpose cluster*using the UI, CLI, or REST API. You can manually terminate and restart an all-purpose cluster. Multiple users can share such clusters to do collaborative interactive analysis.
- The Databricks job scheduler creates *a job cluster*when you run a job on a*new job cluster*and terminates the cluster when the job is complete. You*cannot*restart an job cluster.

A set of idle, ready-to-use instances that reduce cluster start and auto-scaling times. When attached to a pool, a cluster allocates its driver and worker nodes from the pool. See Pool configuration reference.

If the pool does not have sufficient idle resources to accommodate the cluster's request, the pool expands by allocating new instances from the instance provider. When an attached cluster is terminated, the instances it used are returned to the pool and can be reused by a different cluster.

reference_note.title: Databricks Data Organization and Compute Fundamentals
reference_note.summary: Databricks organizes data using a hierarchy of Catalogs → Schemas → Tables/Volumes, with Unity Catalog managing metadata and permissions across your account. You run code on Clusters, which are compute resources that can be shared (all-purpose) or created temporarily for jobs (job clusters). Understanding this structure and how to access data through Unity Catalog instead of deprecated DBFS is essential for any real project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The top-level container that holds all your data and AI assets. Think of it as a folder that can be shared across workspaces in the same region and account.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Catalogs let you organize and isolate data logically, and share it across teams and workspaces without duplicating it.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A container inside a Catalog that provides more detailed organization. Schemas hold tables, volumes, functions, and models.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Schemas let you group related data objects together, making it easier to find and manage data in larger projects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A structured data object that you query using SQL or Spark APIs. By default, all Databricks tables are Delta tables.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tables are the main way you store and query structured data in Databricks. Delta tables provide ACID guarantees and high performance.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A table format based on Delta Lake that stores data as files on cloud storage and registers metadata in the metastore. Provides ACID transactions and reliability.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Delta tables are the standard in Databricks and give you data reliability, consistency, and performance out of the box.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A logical storage location for non-tabular data (files, images, documents, etc.). Volumes organize and control access to unstructured data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If your project needs to store files or non-structured data, volumes are the recommended way to manage and secure that data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A read-only object that saves a query result derived from one or more tables or other views. You query it like a table, but it doesn't store data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Views let you create reusable query definitions and simplify complex queries for other users without duplicating data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: An account-level system that manages metadata, permissions, and access control for all data, AI assets, and catalogs. It replaces the legacy Hive metastore.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Unity Catalog is the modern way to govern data access, track permissions, and manage data across your entire Databricks account. You should use it instead of DBFS.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A central registry that stores metadata about your catalogs, schemas, tables, and permissions. Unity Catalog provides an account-level metastore.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: The metastore tracks what data exists, where it is, and who can access it. This is essential for data governance in real projects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A set of compute resources (machines) and configurations where you run notebooks and jobs. Two types: all-purpose (shared, manual control) and job (temporary, auto-created).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You need a cluster to execute any code in Databricks. Choosing the right cluster type affects cost, collaboration, and job automation.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A cluster you create and manage manually. Multiple users can share it for interactive analysis. You can stop and restart it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Use all-purpose clusters for development, exploration, and collaborative work where you need flexibility and want to save costs by sharing resources.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A cluster created automatically by the Databricks job scheduler when a job runs, then terminated when the job finishes. You cannot restart it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Job clusters are used for automated workflows and scheduled jobs. They reduce costs because they only exist while the job is running.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A set of idle, pre-initialized compute instances that clusters can use. Reduces cluster startup time and auto-scaling delays.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Pools speed up cluster creation and scaling, which is useful if you run many jobs or need fast cluster startup in production.

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A UI tool that lets you browse and manage all your data and AI assets (schemas, tables, models, volumes, functions). You can find data objects, understand relationships, and manage permissions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use Catalog Explorer when you need to explore what data exists, find data owners, understand table relationships, or manage who can access what.

important_features_or_tools.name: Unity Catalog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Account-level metadata management and access control system. Registers and governs all catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes, and permissions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always use Unity Catalog for managing data access and permissions in real projects. It is the modern standard and replaces the legacy Hive metastore.

important_features_or_tools.name: Hive Metastore (Legacy)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The older metadata management system for Databricks. Still available for customers who have not adopted Unity Catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Only use if you are on a legacy Databricks setup. For new projects, use Unity Catalog instead.

important_features_or_tools.name: DBFS (Deprecated)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Databricks File System. A storage location available to all users by default. Storing and accessing data via DBFS root or DBFS mounts is deprecated.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Do not use DBFS for new projects. Use Unity Catalog and Volumes instead to manage data access.

important_features_or_tools.name: All-Purpose Cluster
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A cluster you create and manage. Can be shared by multiple users. You can manually terminate and restart it.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use for interactive development, exploration, and collaborative analysis where you need control and want to share compute resources.

important_parameters.meaning: How you create the cluster

important_features_or_tools.name: Job Cluster
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A cluster automatically created by the Databricks job scheduler when a job runs. Automatically terminates when the job completes. Cannot be restarted.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use for automated jobs and scheduled workflows. Reduces costs because the cluster only exists during job execution.

important_parameters.meaning: Option to run a job on a newly created cluster instead of an existing one

important_features_or_tools.name: Pool
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A set of idle, ready-to-use compute instances. When a cluster is attached to a pool, it allocates driver and worker nodes from the pool. If the pool lacks resources, it expands by requesting new instances.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use pools to reduce cluster startup time and auto-scaling delays, especially for jobs that run frequently or need fast scaling.

important_parameters.meaning: Pre-initialized instances in the pool ready for immediate use
The cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) that supplies new instances when the pool expands

practical_workflow.action: Set up Unity Catalog for your account if not already done. This is your data governance foundation.
practical_workflow.reason: Unity Catalog manages all metadata and permissions. It is the modern standard and required for secure data management in real projects.

practical_workflow.action: Create or identify a Catalog for your project. Decide if you need to share it across workspaces.
practical_workflow.reason: Catalogs are the top-level container. Organizing by project or team makes data easier to find and manage.

practical_workflow.action: Create Schemas (databases) within your Catalog to organize related data objects.
practical_workflow.reason: Schemas provide granular organization. Group related tables, volumes, and functions together logically.

practical_workflow.action: Create Tables for structured data or Volumes for non-tabular data (files, images, etc.).
practical_workflow.reason: Tables and Volumes are where your actual data lives. Tables are queried with SQL; Volumes store unstructured data.

practical_workflow.action: Create an all-purpose cluster for interactive development and exploration.
practical_workflow.reason: You need compute resources to run code. All-purpose clusters are ideal for development and team collaboration.

practical_workflow.action: Use Catalog Explorer to browse your data, understand relationships, and verify permissions.
practical_workflow.reason: Catalog Explorer is your main tool for discovering and managing data assets. Use it to verify everything is organized correctly.

practical_workflow.action: For production jobs, create job clusters or attach jobs to existing clusters. Use Pools if you run many jobs.
practical_workflow.reason: Job clusters automate compute lifecycle and reduce costs. Pools speed up job execution by pre-initializing instances.

practical_workflow.action: Query tables using Apache Spark SQL or Spark APIs. Create views for reusable queries.
practical_workflow.reason: Tables are the main data objects you query. Views save complex queries and simplify access for other users.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using DBFS root or DBFS mounts to store and access data.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use Unity Catalog, Volumes, and Tables instead. DBFS is deprecated and does not provide proper access control or governance.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking a job cluster can be restarted or reused.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Job clusters are temporary. They are created when a job runs and terminated when it finishes. Use all-purpose clusters if you need to restart and reuse.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing Schemas with Catalogs.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Catalogs are the top level (account-wide, shareable across workspaces). Schemas are inside Catalogs and provide more detailed organization.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking Views store data like Tables.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Views are read-only and derived from Tables. They save query definitions but do not store data themselves.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using the legacy Hive metastore for new projects.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use Unity Catalog instead. It is the modern standard and provides better governance, security, and features.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not using Pools when running many jobs.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Pools reduce cluster startup time and auto-scaling delays. If your project runs frequent jobs, Pools can save time and cost.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, start by setting up Unity Catalog and creating a Catalog for your project. This ensures proper data governance from day one.
Use Schemas to organize tables by domain or business function (e.g., 'sales', 'marketing', 'finance'). This makes data discovery easier for your team.
Always use Tables for structured data and Volumes for files or unstructured data. Do not use DBFS.
Create an all-purpose cluster for your team's interactive work. This allows collaboration and reduces compute costs by sharing resources.
Use Catalog Explorer regularly to understand your data landscape, find data owners, and verify permissions are correct.
For production workflows, use job clusters or attach jobs to existing clusters. If you run many jobs, set up a Pool to speed up execution.
Create Views for commonly used queries. This saves time for other team members and reduces query complexity.
Remember that all tables created in Databricks are Delta tables by default. You get ACID guarantees and high performance without extra configuration.

The set of core components that run on the clusters managed by Databricks. See Compute. Databricks has the following runtimes:

- Databricks Runtime includes Apache Spark but also adds a number of components and updates that substantially improve the usability, performance, and security of big data analytics.
- Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning is built on Databricks Runtime and provides prebuilt machine learning infrastructure that is integrated with all of the capabilities of the Databricks workspace. It contains multiple popular libraries, including TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch, and XGBoost.

The **Jobs & Pipelines** workspace UI provides entry to the Jobs, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, and Lakeflow Connect UIs, which are tools that allow you to orchestrate and schedule workflows.

A non-interactive mechanism for orchestrating and scheduling notebooks, libraries, and other tasks. See Lakeflow Jobs

Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines provide a declarative framework for building reliable, maintainable, and testable data processing pipelines. See Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines.

Workload is the amount of processing capability needed to perform a task or group of tasks. Databricks identifies two types of workloads: data engineering (job) and data analytics (all-purpose).

- **Data engineering**An (automated) workload runs on- *a job cluster*which the Databricks job scheduler creates for each workload.
- **Data analytics**An (interactive) workload runs on an- *all-purpose cluster*. Interactive workloads typically run commands within a Databricks notebook. However, running a- *job*on an- *existing all-purpose*cluster is also treated as an interactive workload.

The state for a read–eval–print loop (REPL) environment for each supported programming language. The languages supported are Python, R, Scala, and SQL.

Data engineering tools aid collaboration among data scientists, data engineers, data analysts, and machine learning engineers.

A workspace is an environment for accessing all of your Databricks assets. A workspace organizes objects (notebooks, libraries, dashboards, and experiments) into folders and provides access to data objects and computational resources.

A web-based interface for creating data science and machine learning workflows that can contain runnable commands, visualizations, and narrative text. See Databricks notebooks.

A package of code available to the notebook or job running on your cluster. Databricks runtimes include many libraries, and you can also upload your own. See Install libraries.

A folder whose contents are co-versioned together by syncing them to a remote Git repository. Databricks Git folders integrate with Git to provide source and version control for your projects.

Databricks provides an integrated end-to-end environment with managed services for developing and deploying AI and machine learning applications.

To help you develop ML and AI models, Databricks provides a Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning, which automates compute creation with pre-built machine learning and deep learning infrastructure including the most common ML and DL libraries. It also has built-in, pre-configured GPU support including drivers and supporting libraries. Browse to information about the latest runtime releases from Databricks Runtime release notes versions and compatibility.

reference_note.title: Databricks Core Components: Runtimes, Workloads, and Workspace Fundamentals
reference_note.summary: Databricks provides managed runtimes (standard and ML-focused) that run on clusters you don't have to manage yourself. You organize your work in a workspace using notebooks, and you run either data engineering jobs (automated, on job clusters) or data analytics work (interactive, on all-purpose clusters). Understanding these core pieces helps you set up and run projects quickly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A pre-configured software environment that runs on your cluster. It includes Apache Spark plus Databricks improvements for performance, usability, and security. You don't install or manage it—Databricks handles it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You get a working Spark environment immediately without setup overhead. When you create a cluster, you choose which runtime to use based on your task.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A specialized runtime built on top of Databricks Runtime. It comes pre-loaded with ML libraries like TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch, and XGBoost, plus GPU support.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If you're building ML models, this runtime saves you from installing libraries manually. It's ready to use for ML work immediately.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Your Databricks environment. It's where you store and organize notebooks, libraries, dashboards, and experiments in folders. It also connects you to your data and compute resources.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Everything you create in Databricks lives in a workspace. It's your project hub.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks recognizes two kinds of work: data engineering (automated jobs) and data analytics (interactive exploration). Each runs on a different type of cluster.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Knowing your workload type determines how you set up and run your code, and affects cost and resource management.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A job cluster is created automatically by Databricks when you run a scheduled job, then deleted when done. An all-purpose cluster stays running and is used for interactive notebook work.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Job clusters are cheaper for automated tasks; all-purpose clusters are better for exploration and development where you need the cluster to stay available.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks Notebook
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A web-based interface where you write and run code. Notebooks support Python, R, Scala, and SQL. You can mix code, visualizations, and text explanations in one document.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use notebooks for data exploration, analysis, ML model development, and any interactive work. They're the primary way you interact with Databricks.

important_features_or_tools.name: Jobs & Pipelines UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A workspace section that provides access to Jobs, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, and Lakeflow Connect. These tools let you schedule and orchestrate workflows automatically.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this when you need to run notebooks or tasks on a schedule, or when you want to build automated data pipelines that run without manual intervention.

important_features_or_tools.name: Lakeflow Jobs
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A non-interactive mechanism for orchestrating and scheduling notebooks, libraries, and other tasks. Jobs run on job clusters that are created and destroyed automatically.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use jobs for automated, scheduled data engineering tasks like ETL pipelines or model retraining that run on a schedule.

important_features_or_tools.name: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A declarative framework for building data processing pipelines. You define pipelines in a declarative way (describing what you want, not how to do it), making them reliable, maintainable, and testable.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this when building production data pipelines that need to be reliable and easy to maintain over time.

important_features_or_tools.name: Libraries
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Packages of code available to notebooks or jobs running on your cluster. Databricks runtimes include many libraries pre-installed. You can also upload your own custom libraries.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use pre-installed libraries for common tasks. Upload custom libraries when you have reusable code you want to share across notebooks or jobs.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks Git Folders
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A folder in your workspace whose contents are synced with a remote Git repository. Provides version control and source control for your projects.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use Git folders when working on team projects or when you need version history and collaboration features.

important_features_or_tools.name: REPL (Read–Eval–Print Loop)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: An interactive environment in notebooks that supports Python, R, Scala, and SQL. You write code, it executes, and you see results immediately.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this for interactive exploration and development. It's the default way notebooks work.

practical_workflow.action: Access your Databricks workspace and create or open a notebook
practical_workflow.reason: Notebooks are where you write and test your code. This is your starting point for any project.

practical_workflow.action: Choose a runtime when creating a cluster. Use Databricks Runtime for general work, or Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning if building ML models.
practical_workflow.reason: The runtime determines what libraries and tools are available. Choosing the right one saves setup time.

practical_workflow.action: Write and test your code interactively in the notebook using the REPL environment
practical_workflow.reason: Interactive development lets you iterate quickly and see results immediately.

practical_workflow.action: Once your code is working, decide if it needs to run on a schedule. If yes, create a Job from the Jobs & Pipelines UI.
practical_workflow.reason: Jobs automate recurring tasks and run on job clusters, which are cost-effective for scheduled work.

practical_workflow.action: For complex data pipelines, consider using Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines instead of Jobs
practical_workflow.reason: Declarative pipelines are more maintainable and testable for production data workflows.

practical_workflow.action: If working with a team, set up a Databricks Git folder to sync your notebooks with a Git repository
practical_workflow.reason: Version control and collaboration are essential for team projects.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to install and manage Spark yourself
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Databricks Runtime handles this for you. When you create a cluster, Spark is already there and configured.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using an all-purpose cluster for scheduled jobs to save money
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use job clusters for scheduled work—they're created on-demand and deleted after the job finishes, which is cheaper. All-purpose clusters are for interactive work.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not realizing ML libraries are pre-installed in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you're doing ML work, use the ML runtime. TensorFlow, PyTorch, XGBoost, and others are already there. No pip install needed.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing Jobs with Notebooks
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Notebooks are interactive tools for development. Jobs are automated, scheduled executions of notebooks or code. Use notebooks to develop, then wrap them in jobs for production.

project_usage_notes: Start with a notebook on an all-purpose cluster to explore your data and develop your solution interactively.
Once your code works, convert it to a Job if it needs to run on a schedule (e.g., daily ETL, weekly model retraining).
If building ML models, create your cluster with Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning to get TensorFlow, PyTorch, and GPU support out of the box.
Use Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines for production data pipelines that multiple team members will maintain.
Store your notebooks in a Git folder if working with a team to enable version control and collaboration.
Remember: all-purpose clusters stay running (good for development), job clusters are created and destroyed per job (good for cost-effective automation).

A collection of MLflow runs for developing agents, LLM applications, and ML models. See Organize training runs with MLflow experiments.

Features are an important component of ML models. A feature store enables feature sharing and discovery across your organization and also ensures that the same feature computation code is used for model training and inference. See Databricks Feature Store.

Databricks supports the exploration, development, and deployment of generative AI models, including:

- AI playground, a chat-like environment in the workspace where you can test, prompt, and compare LLMs. See Chat with LLMs and prototype generative AI apps using AI Playground.
- A built-in set of pre-configured foundation models that you can query:
- See Pay-per-token Foundation Model APIs.
- See [Recommended] Deploy foundation models from Unity Catalog for foundation models you can serve with a single click.

- Third-party hosted LLMs, called external models. These models are meant to be used as-is.
- Capabilities to customize a foundation model to optimize its performance for your specific application (often called fine-tuning). See Foundation Model Fine-tuning (deprecated).

Databricks provides a hosted version of MLflow Model Registry in Unity Catalog. Models registered in Unity Catalog inherit centralized access control, lineage, and cross-workspace discovery and access. See Manage model lifecycle in Unity Catalog.

Model Serving provides a unified interface to deploy, govern, and query AI models. Each model you serve is available as a REST API that you can integrate into your web or client application. With Model Serving, you can deploy your own models, foundation models, or third-party models hosted outside of Databricks. See Deploy models using Model Serving.

Data warehousing refers to collecting and storing data from multiple sources so it can be quickly accessed for business insights and reporting. Databricks SQL is the collection of services that bring data warehousing capabilities and performance to your existing data lakes. See Data warehousing architecture.

A query is a valid SQL statement that allows you to interact with your data. You can author queries using the in-platform SQL editor, or connect using a SQL connector, driver, or API. See Access and manage saved queries to learn more about how to work with queries.

A computation resource on which you run SQL queries. There are three types of SQL warehouses: Classic, Pro, and Serverless. Databricks recommends using serverless warehouses where available. See SQL warehouse types to compare available features for each warehouse type.

A list of executed queries and their performance characteristics. Query history allows you to monitor query performance, helping you identify bottlenecks and optimize query runtimes. See Query history.

A graphical presentation of the result of running a query. See Visualizations in Databricks notebooks and SQL editor.

A presentation of data visualizations and commentary. You can use dashboards to automatically send reports to anyone in your Databricks account. Use the Genie Code to help you build visualizations based on natural language prompts. See Dashboards. You can also create a dashboard from a notebook. See Dashboards in Databricks notebooks.

reference_note.title: Databricks ML, AI, and Data Warehousing Core Features
reference_note.summary: Databricks provides integrated tools for machine learning (MLflow experiments and model registry), generative AI development (AI Playground, foundation models, model serving), and data warehousing (SQL queries, warehouses, dashboards). You can organize training runs, manage models with centralized access control, deploy AI models as REST APIs, and analyze data with SQL—all in one platform.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A way to organize and track multiple machine learning training runs so you can compare results and manage your model development process.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When building ML models, you run many experiments with different parameters. MLflow helps you keep track of all of them in one place.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A centralized place to store and manage features (the input variables used in ML models). The same feature code is used for both training and making predictions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Ensures consistency between training and production, and lets your team reuse features across different projects instead of rebuilding them.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) provided by Databricks that you can use immediately without training from scratch.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you build generative AI applications quickly without the cost and complexity of training your own LLM.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A centralized system for storing, versioning, and managing ML models with built-in access control and the ability to share models across your organization.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Keeps your models organized, secure, and discoverable across teams and workspaces in your company.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A service that turns your trained models into REST APIs so applications can call them to make predictions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Bridges the gap between model development and real-world use—your app or website can query the model over the internet.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A computation resource that runs SQL queries on your data lake, similar to a traditional data warehouse but built on Databricks.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you query and analyze large amounts of data quickly for business reporting and insights.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Visual presentations of query results and charts that you can share with others and automatically send as reports.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Turns raw data into easy-to-understand visuals that stakeholders can use to make decisions.

important_features_or_tools.name: AI Playground
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A chat-like environment in the Databricks workspace where you can test, prompt, and compare different large language models (LLMs) interactively.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to quickly experiment with LLMs and prototype generative AI applications before building them into your project.

important_features_or_tools.name: Pay-per-token Foundation Model APIs
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Pre-configured foundation models available through Databricks that you can query and pay only for the tokens (words) you use.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to use a foundation model in your application and want a simple, cost-effective way to access it.

important_features_or_tools.name: Deploy foundation models from Unity Catalog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to serve foundation models with a single click, making them available as REST APIs for your applications.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to deploy a foundation model to production quickly without complex setup.

important_features_or_tools.name: External Models
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Third-party hosted LLMs that are used as-is without modification or fine-tuning.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to use an LLM from another provider (like OpenAI) directly in your Databricks workflow.

important_features_or_tools.name: Foundation Model Fine-tuning
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Capabilities to customize a foundation model to perform better on your specific use case (deprecated feature).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When a pre-trained foundation model doesn't perform well enough for your specific task and you want to customize it.

important_features_or_tools.name: Model Serving
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A unified interface to deploy, govern, and query AI models. Each deployed model becomes a REST API endpoint.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you have a trained model and need to make it available to applications or users over the internet.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks SQL
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A collection of services that bring data warehousing capabilities to your data lake, allowing you to run SQL queries and analyze data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to query, analyze, and report on large amounts of data stored in your data lake.

important_features_or_tools.name: SQL Editor
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: An in-platform editor where you can write and execute SQL queries against your data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to write and run SQL queries directly in Databricks without using external tools.

important_features_or_tools.name: SQL Warehouse
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A computation resource that executes SQL queries. Available in three types: Classic, Pro, and Serverless.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Every time you run a SQL query—you need a warehouse to provide the computing power.

important_parameters.meaning: Determines the features and performance characteristics available. Options are Classic, Pro, or Serverless.

important_features_or_tools.name: Query History
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A list of all executed queries and their performance metrics (execution time, resource usage, etc.).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to monitor query performance, identify slow queries, and optimize them.

important_features_or_tools.name: Visualizations
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Graphical presentations of query results (charts, graphs, tables) that help you understand data visually.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to present query results in a visual format that's easier to understand than raw data.

important_features_or_tools.name: Dashboards
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A presentation of data visualizations and commentary that can be shared and automatically sent as reports to team members.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to create a central place for stakeholders to view key metrics and insights, or send regular reports.

important_features_or_tools.name: Genie Code
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A tool that helps you build visualizations based on natural language prompts instead of writing code manually.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to create visualizations quickly by describing what you want in plain English.

This tutorial provides a quick walkthrough of creating a table and granting privileges in Databricks using the Unity Catalog data governance model. As of November 8, 2023, workspaces in new accounts are automatically enabled for Unity Catalog and include the permissions required for all users to complete this tutorial.

If you are unsure if your workspace is enabled for Unity Catalog, see Get started with Unity Catalog. If you would like to familiarize yourself with Unity Catalog data objects, see What is Unity Catalog?.

This article is intended for users but may also be of interest to admins who are newly responsible for workspace management.

In order to perform the tasks described in this article, you must have:

- A Databricks workspace that was enabled for Unity Catalog automatically.
- Permissions to attach to a compute resource. See Classic compute overview.

Unity Catalog includes a three-level namespace for data objects: `catalog.schema.table`. In this example, you'll run a notebook that creates a table named `department` in the workspace catalog and `default` schema (database).

The workspace catalog is the default catalog created with your workspace that all users have access to. It shares a name with your workspace.

You can define access to tables declaratively using SQL or the Databricks Explorer UI:

-
In the sidebar, click **+New**>**Notebook**.
-
Select `SQL`as your notebook language.
-
Click **Connect**and attach the notebook to a compute resource.
-
Add the following commands to the notebook and run them (replace `<workspace-catalog>`with the name of your workspace catalog):SQL`USE CATALOG <workspace-catalog>`SQL`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS default.department`
 (
 deptcode INT,
 deptname STRING,
 location STRING
 );SQL`INSERT INTO default.department VALUES`
 (10, 'FINANCE', 'EDINBURGH'),
 (20, 'SOFTWARE', 'PADDINGTON');
-
In the sidebar, click **Catalog**and then search for the workspace catalog (`<workspace-name>`) and the`default`schema, where you'll find your new`department`table.

As the original table creator, you're the table *owner*, and you can grant other users permission to read or write to the table. You can even transfer ownership, but we won't do that here. For more information about the Unity Catalog privileges and permissions model, see Manage privileges in Unity Catalog.

To give users permissions on your table using the UI:

- Click the table name in Catalog Explorer to open the table details page, and go to the **Permissions**tab.
- Click **Grant**.
- On the **Grant on**dialog:- Select the users and groups you want to give permission to.
- Select the privileges you want to grant. For this example, assign the `SELECT`(read) privilege and click**Grant**.

You can also grant those permissions using the following SQL statement in a Databricks notebook or the SQL query editor. In this example, you give a group called `data-consumers` permissions on your table:

```
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE default.department TO `data-consumers`;
```

As the table creator, you become the owner and can grant read or write permissions to other users and groups.

This tutorial explains how to create and deploy an ETL (extract, transform, and load) pipeline for data orchestration using Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines and Auto Loader. An ETL pipeline implements the steps to read data from source systems, transform that data based on requirements, such as data quality checks and record de-duplication, and write the data to a target system, such as a data warehouse or a data lake.

In this tutorial, you will use pipelines and Auto Loader to:

- Ingest raw source data into a target table.
- Transform the raw source data and write the transformed data to two target materialized views.
- Query the transformed data.
- Automate the ETL pipeline with a Databricks job.

For more information about pipelines and Auto Loader, see Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines and What is Auto Loader?

To complete this tutorial, you must meet the following requirements:

- Be logged into a Databricks workspace.
- Have Unity Catalog enabled for your workspace.
- Have serverless compute enabled for your account. Serverless Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines are not available in all workspace regions. See Features with limited regional availability for available regions.
- Have permission to create a compute resource or access to a compute resource.
- Have permissions to create a new schema in a catalog. The required permissions are `USE CATALOG`and`CREATE SCHEMA`.
- Have permissions to create a new volume in an existing schema. The required permissions are `USE SCHEMA`and`CREATE VOLUME`.

The dataset used in this example is a subset of the Million Song Dataset, a collection of features and metadata for contemporary music tracks. This dataset is available in the sample datasets included in your Databricks workspace.

First, create a pipeline by defining the datasets in files (called *source code*) using pipeline syntax. Each source code file can contain only one language, but you can add multiple language-specific files in the pipeline. To learn more, see Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines

This tutorial uses serverless compute and Unity Catalog. For all configuration options that are not specified, use the default settings. If serverless compute is not enabled or supported in your workspace, you can complete the tutorial as written using default compute settings.

To create a new pipeline, follow these steps:

- In your workspace, click  **New**in the sidebar, then select**ETL Pipeline**. This opens the pipeline editor with a default pipeline name like`New Pipeline <date> <time>`.
- (Optional) Select the name and enter a descriptive name for the pipeline.
- (Optional) To the right of the name, click the catalog and schema to set different defaults.
- (Optional) In the `my_transformation`source file created for you, select**Python**or**SQL**from the language drop-down list to set the language for the file.
- Click  **Use sample code**.

Sample code in your selected language appears in the `my_transformation` file in the `transformations` folder.

reference_note.title: Creating and Deploying ETL Pipelines with Lakeflow and Auto Loader
reference_note.summary: An ETL pipeline automates the process of reading data from sources, transforming it (cleaning, deduplicating, quality checks), and writing it to a target system. Databricks provides Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines and Auto Loader to build these pipelines. This tutorial teaches you to ingest raw data, transform it into materialized views, query results, and automate the pipeline with a Databricks job.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A three-step automated process: Extract (read data from source systems), Transform (clean, deduplicate, validate data quality), and Load (write processed data to a target system like a data warehouse or data lake).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ETL pipelines are the foundation of data engineering projects. They automate repetitive data processing tasks, ensure data quality, and make data ready for analysis.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks feature that lets you define data pipelines using declarative syntax (you describe what you want, not how to do it) in Python or SQL source code files.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Declarative pipelines are easier to read, maintain, and version control than imperative code. Each source file contains one language and defines transformation logic.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks feature that automatically detects and ingests new data files from source systems into target tables as they arrive.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Auto Loader eliminates manual file discovery and ingestion, making your pipeline truly automated and responsive to new data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Pre-computed query results stored as tables. In this tutorial, transformed data is written to two materialized views for downstream querying.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Materialized views improve query performance by pre-computing expensive transformations, so analysts can query results quickly without recomputing.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks' centralized governance system for managing data access, permissions, and metadata across your workspace.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Unity Catalog is required for this tutorial and ensures proper data governance and access control in production projects.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Each source code file can contain only one language (Python or SQL). If you need multiple languages, create separate source files for each language.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, use Auto Loader to ingest raw data from your actual source system (e.g., cloud storage, APIs). The tutorial uses sample datasets, but the pattern applies to production data.

Define transformation logic in source files based on your data quality requirements. The tutorial shows the pattern; customize it for your specific business rules (deduplication, validation, filtering).
Materialized views are ideal for downstream analytics. Store transformed data in materialized views so analysts can query results without recomputing expensive transformations.
Always test your pipeline with sample data before automating it with a Databricks job. Use the query step to verify transformations are correct.
Once tested, automate the pipeline with a Databricks job so it runs on a schedule (daily, hourly) or when new data arrives. This eliminates manual execution.
Use Unity Catalog to manage permissions and governance. Ensure only authorized users can access raw and transformed data.
If serverless compute is not available in your region, you can complete the same workflow using default compute settings (you'll manage a compute cluster instead).

 from pyspark import pipelines as dp
 from pyspark.sql.functions import *
 from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType, IntegerType, StringType, StructType, StructField

schema = StructType(
 [
 StructField("artist_id", StringType(), True),
 StructField("artist_lat", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("artist_long", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("artist_location", StringType(), True),
 StructField("artist_name", StringType(), True),
 StructField("duration", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("end_of_fade_in", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("key", IntegerType(), True),
 StructField("key_confidence", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("loudness", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("release", StringType(), True),
 StructField("song_hotnes", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("song_id", StringType(), True),
 StructField("start_of_fade_out", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("tempo", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("time_signature", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("time_signature_confidence", DoubleType(), True),
 StructField("title", StringType(), True),
 StructField("year", IntegerType(), True),
 StructField("partial_sequence", IntegerType(), True)
 ]
 )
 @dp.table(
 comment="Raw data from a subset of the Million Song Dataset; a collection of features and metadata for contemporary music tracks."
 )
 def songs_raw():
 return (spark.readStream
 .format("cloudFiles")
 .schema(schema)
 .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
 .option("sep","\t")
 .load(file_path))

@dp.materialized_view(
 comment="Million Song Dataset with data cleaned and prepared for analysis."
 )
 @dp.expect("valid_artist_name", "artist_name IS NOT NULL")
 @dp.expect("valid_title", "song_title IS NOT NULL")
 @dp.expect("valid_duration", "duration > 0")
 def songs_prepared():
 return (
 spark.read.table("songs_raw")
 .withColumnRenamed("title", "song_title")
 .select("artist_id", "artist_name", "duration", "release", "tempo", "time_signature", "song_title", "year")
 )

@dp.materialized_view(
 comment="A table summarizing counts of songs released by the artists who released the most songs each year."
 )
 def top_artists_by_year():
 return (
 spark.read.table("songs_prepared")
 .filter(expr("year > 0"))
 .groupBy("artist_name", "year")
 .count().withColumnRenamed("count", "total_number_of_songs")
 .sort(desc("total_number_of_songs"), desc("year"))
 )SQL`-- Define a streaming table to ingest data from a volume`
 CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE songs_raw
 COMMENT "Raw data from a subset of the Million Song Dataset; a collection of features and metadata for contemporary music tracks."
 AS SELECT *
 FROM STREAM read_files(
 '/databricks-datasets/songs/data-001/part*',
 format => "csv",
 header => "false",
 delimiter => "\t",
 schema => """
 artist_id STRING,
 artist_lat DOUBLE,
 artist_long DOUBLE,
 artist_location STRING,
 artist_name STRING,
 duration DOUBLE,
 end_of_fade_in DOUBLE,
 key INT,
 key_confidence DOUBLE,
 loudness DOUBLE,
 release STRING,
 song_hotnes DOUBLE,
 song_id STRING,
 start_of_fade_out DOUBLE,
 tempo DOUBLE,
 time_signature INT,
 time_signature_confidence DOUBLE,
 title STRING,
 year INT,
 partial_sequence STRING
 """,
 schemaEvolutionMode => "none");
 -- Define a materialized view that validates data and renames a column
 CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW songs_prepared(
 CONSTRAINT valid_artist_name EXPECT (artist_name IS NOT NULL),
 CONSTRAINT valid_title EXPECT (song_title IS NOT NULL),
 CONSTRAINT valid_duration EXPECT (duration > 0)
 )
 COMMENT "Million Song Dataset with data cleaned and prepared for analysis."
 AS SELECT artist_id, artist_name, duration, release, tempo, time_signature, title AS song_title, year
 FROM songs_raw;
 -- Define a materialized view that has a filtered, aggregated, and sorted view of the data
 CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW top_artists_by_year
 COMMENT "A table summarizing counts of songs released by the artists each year, who released the most songs."
 AS SELECT
 artist_name,
 year,
 COUNT(*) AS total_number_of_songs
 FROM songs_prepared
 WHERE year > 0
 GROUP BY artist_name, year
 ORDER BY total_number_of_songs DESC, year DESC;This source includes code for three queries. You could also put those queries in separate files, to organize the files and code the way that you prefer.

Click **Run file**or**Run pipeline**to start an update for the connected pipeline. With only one source file in your pipeline, these are functionally equivalent.

When the update completes, the editor is updated with information about your pipeline.

- The pipeline graph, also called the directed acyclic graph (DAG), in the sidebar to the right of your code, shows three tables, `songs_raw`,`songs_prepared`, and`top_artists_by_year`.
- A summary of the update is shown at the top of the pipeline asset browser.
- Details of the tables that were generated are shown in the bottom pane, and you can browse data from the tables by selecting one.

This includes the raw and cleaned up data, as well as some simple analysis to find the top artists by year. In the next step, you create ad-hoc queries for further analysis in a separate file in your pipeline.

reference_note.title: Databricks Lakehouse Development: Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Pipelines
reference_note.summary: Databricks lets you build data pipelines using Streaming Tables (for ingesting raw data), Materialized Views (for cleaning and transforming data), and Python decorators. You define these objects once, and Databricks automatically maintains them. Pipelines visualize your data flow as a DAG and let you run updates with a single click. This approach lets you quickly move from raw data to analysis-ready tables.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A table that automatically ingests and updates data from a source (like files in a volume). You define it once with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE, and Databricks keeps it up-to-date as new data arrives.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In a real project, you need a reliable way to ingest raw data continuously. Streaming Tables handle this automatically without manual refresh logic.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A table that stores the results of a query. Unlike a regular view, it pre-computes and stores the results, so queries run faster. You define it with CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When you need cleaned, validated, or aggregated data for analysis, materialized views ensure the data is always ready and fast to query.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A visual representation of how your data flows from one table to another. Databricks automatically tracks dependencies: if songs_raw changes, songs_prepared updates, which then updates top_artists_by_year.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Pipelines show you the complete data lineage and automate updates across all dependent tables, so you don't manually manage refresh order.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Rules you define on a materialized view (like CONSTRAINT valid_artist_name EXPECT (artist_name IS NOT NULL)) that validate data quality. If data violates a constraint, Databricks alerts you.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In production, bad data causes downstream problems. Constraints catch data quality issues early before they propagate.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Defines a table that ingests data from a source (like files in a volume). The STREAM keyword tells Databricks to treat this as a streaming source.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to ingest raw data from external sources (files, APIs, message queues) into Databricks.

important_parameters.meaning: File format of the source data
Whether the source file has a header row
Character that separates fields in the file
Defines the column names and data types for the ingested data
important_parameters.example_value: artist_id STRING, artist_name STRING, duration DOUBLE, ...

important_parameters.meaning: Controls how the table handles schema changes in the source data

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Defines a table that stores pre-computed query results. Automatically updates when source tables change.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to clean, validate, transform, or aggregate data for downstream analysis or reporting.

important_parameters.meaning: Defines a data quality rule with a name and an EXPECT clause that must be true
important_parameters.example_value: CONSTRAINT valid_artist_name EXPECT (artist_name IS NOT NULL)

important_parameters.meaning: Describes what the view contains and why
important_parameters.example_value: Million Song Dataset with data cleaned and prepared for analysis.

important_features_or_tools.name: @dp.materialized_view (Python decorator)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Python-based way to define a materialized view. You write a Python function that returns a Spark DataFrame, and Databricks converts it to a materialized view.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you prefer writing transformations in Python instead of SQL, or when you want to use Python libraries in your data pipeline.

important_parameters.meaning: Describes the purpose of the materialized view
important_parameters.example_value: A table summarizing counts of songs released by the artists who released the most songs each year.

important_features_or_tools.name: read_files()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Reads files from a Databricks volume or external location. Used inside STREAM to ingest data into a Streaming Table.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When your raw data is stored as files (CSV, Parquet, JSON, etc.) in a volume.

important_parameters.meaning: Location of the files to read (supports wildcards like /path/part*)
File format

important_features_or_tools.name: Run file / Run pipeline
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Executes all queries in your pipeline file and updates all Streaming Tables and Materialized Views. Shows a summary of the update and displays the DAG.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After writing or modifying your pipeline code, click 'Run pipeline' to test and execute it.

important_features_or_tools.name: Pipeline graph (DAG sidebar)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Visual representation showing all tables in your pipeline and how they depend on each other. Shows which tables feed into which.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this to understand data lineage and verify that your pipeline structure is correct.

important_features_or_tools.name: Pipeline asset browser (bottom pane)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Shows details about each table generated by your pipeline. You can select a table to browse its data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After running a pipeline, use this to inspect the raw and transformed data to verify correctness.

practical_workflow.action: Define a Streaming Table using CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE with read_files() to ingest raw data from a volume
practical_workflow.reason: This is your data entry point. You specify the file location, format, schema, and any parsing options.

practical_workflow.action: Define a Materialized View using CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW that reads from the Streaming Table, applies transformations (SELECT, WHERE, column renames), and adds CONSTRAINT rules for data quality
practical_workflow.reason: This cleans and validates your data. Constraints catch bad data early. The materialized view pre-computes results for fast queries.

practical_workflow.action: Define additional Materialized Views that read from the cleaned data and perform aggregations, filtering, or sorting for specific analysis needs
practical_workflow.reason: Each view serves a specific analytical purpose. Databricks automatically maintains dependencies, so if raw data changes, all downstream views update.

practical_workflow.action: Click 'Run pipeline' to execute all queries and generate the tables
practical_workflow.reason: This creates the actual tables in Databricks and shows you the DAG and update summary.

practical_workflow.action: Use the pipeline asset browser to inspect the generated tables and verify data quality
practical_workflow.reason: Before using the data for analysis, confirm that transformations worked correctly and constraints passed.

practical_workflow.action: Create ad-hoc queries in separate files that read from your materialized views for further analysis
practical_workflow.reason: Your pipeline provides clean, validated, analysis-ready data. Ad-hoc queries can now focus on business questions without worrying about data preparation.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking a Materialized View is just a regular SQL view that runs the query every time you query it
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: A Materialized View pre-computes and stores results. Queries are fast because the data is already calculated. Databricks automatically refreshes it when source data changes.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Putting all transformations in a single Materialized View instead of breaking them into logical steps
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Create separate Materialized Views for each logical step (raw → cleaned → aggregated). This makes the pipeline easier to understand, debug, and reuse.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not defining CONSTRAINT rules on materialized views
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Constraints are your safety net. They catch data quality issues early. Always add constraints for critical fields (non-null checks, valid ranges, etc.).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming the pipeline automatically runs on a schedule
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: In this example, you manually click 'Run pipeline'. For production, you would configure a schedule or trigger (not shown in this content).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing the DAG with the actual data flow
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The DAG shows dependencies (which tables feed into which). The actual data flows from Streaming Tables → Materialized Views → Analysis. The DAG helps you understand and debug this flow.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, your pipeline file would start with a Streaming Table that ingests raw data from your data source (files, database, API). This is your single source of truth for raw data.
Add a Materialized View immediately after ingestion to clean and validate data. Use CONSTRAINT rules to enforce data quality. This prevents bad data from propagating downstream.
Create separate Materialized Views for different analytical purposes (e.g., one for top artists by year, one for song duration analysis, etc.). Each view is independent and automatically maintained.
Use the DAG to verify that your pipeline structure is correct. If a table is missing or dependencies are wrong, the DAG will show it.

After your pipeline runs successfully, create ad-hoc SQL or Python queries in separate files that read from your materialized views. These queries can focus on business logic because data preparation is already handled.

If you need to modify a transformation (e.g., add a new column or change a filter), edit the Materialized View definition and re-run the pipeline. Databricks automatically updates all dependent tables.
Use the pipeline asset browser to spot-check data after each run. This catches issues early before they affect downstream analysis.
