In this step, you perform ad-hoc queries on the data processed in the ETL pipeline to analyze the song data in the Databricks SQL Editor. These queries use the prepared records created in the previous step.

First, run a query that finds the artists who have released the most songs each year since 1990.

-
From the pipeline asset browser sidebar, click **Add**then**Exploration**.
-
Enter a **Name**and select**SQL**for the exploration file. A SQL notebook is created in a new`explorations`folder. Files in the`explorations`folder are not run as part of a pipeline update by default. The SQL notebook has cells that you can run together or separately.
-
To create a table of artists that release the most songs in each year after 1990, enter the following code in the new SQL file (if there is sample code in the file, replace it). Because this notebook is not part of the pipeline, it does not use the default catalog and schema. Replace the `<catalog>.<schema>`with the catalog and schema that you used as defaults for the pipeline:SQL`-- Which artists released the most songs each year in 1990 or later?`
 SELECT artist_name, total_number_of_songs, year
 -- replace with the catalog/schema you are using:
 FROM <catalog>.<schema>.top_artists_by_year
 WHERE year >= 1990
 ORDER BY total_number_of_songs DESC, year DESC;
-
Click or press `Shift + Enter`to run this query.

Now, run another query that finds songs with a 4/4 beat and danceable tempo.

-
Add the following code to the next cell in the same file. Again, replace the `<catalog>.<schema>`with the catalog and schema that you used as defaults for the pipeline:SQL`-- Find songs with a 4/4 beat and danceable tempo`
 SELECT artist_name, song_title, tempo
 -- replace with the catalog/schema you are using:
 FROM <catalog>.<schema>.songs_prepared
 WHERE time_signature = 4 AND tempo between 100 and 140;
-
Click or press `Shift + Enter`to run this query.

Next, create a workflow to automate data ingestion, processing, and analysis steps using a Databricks job that runs on a schedule.

- At the top of the editor, choose the **Schedule**button.
- If the **Schedules**dialog appears, choose**Add schedule**.
- This opens the **New schedule**dialog, where you can create a job to run your pipeline on a schedule.
- Optionally, give the job a name.
- By default, the schedule is set to run once per day. You can accept this defaut, or set your own schedule. Choosing **Advanced**gives you the option to set a specific time that the job will run. Selecting**More options**allows you to create notifications when the job runs.
- Select **Create**to apply the changes and create the job.

Now the job will run daily to keep your pipeline up to date. You can choose **Schedule** again to view the list of schedules. You can manage schedules for your pipeline from that dialog, including adding, editing, or removing schedules.

Clicking the name of the schedule (or job) takes you to the job's page in the **Jobs & pipelines** list. From there you can view details about job runs, including the history of runs, or run the job immediately with the **Run now** button.

See Monitor Lakeflow Jobs for more information about job runs.

reference_note.title: Running Ad-Hoc Queries and Scheduling Pipelines in Databricks SQL Editor
reference_note.summary: Learn how to create SQL explorations to analyze processed data using the Databricks SQL Editor, run ad-hoc queries on prepared tables, and automate your entire pipeline by scheduling it as a job that runs on a daily schedule. This workflow lets you query results and keep your data fresh automatically.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A SQL notebook stored in an `explorations` folder that lets you write and run queries against your processed data. Unlike pipeline assets, explorations don't run automatically when the pipeline updates.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Explorations let you analyze and validate your pipeline results without affecting the pipeline itself. You can experiment with queries freely.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: One-time SQL queries you write to answer specific questions about your data, like 'which artists released the most songs each year' or 'which songs have a danceable tempo'.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Ad-hoc queries help you explore, validate, and understand your processed data before deciding what to do with it next.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A way to automatically run your entire pipeline on a fixed schedule (like daily) without manual intervention.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Scheduling keeps your data fresh and up-to-date automatically, so you don't have to manually re-run the pipeline every time you need new results.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When writing queries in explorations, you must explicitly reference your catalog and schema using the format `<catalog>.<schema>.table_name` because explorations don't use the pipeline's default catalog and schema.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Forgetting to replace `<catalog>.<schema>` will cause your queries to fail. This is a key difference between exploration notebooks and pipeline assets.

important_features_or_tools.name: Add > Exploration
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new SQL notebook in the `explorations` folder for writing and running ad-hoc queries against your pipeline's processed data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to analyze, validate, or explore the results of your ETL pipeline without modifying the pipeline itself.

important_features_or_tools.name: SQL Notebook Cells
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Individual SQL query blocks within a SQL notebook that can be run together or separately.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to organize multiple related queries in one file and run them independently or in sequence.

important_features_or_tools.name: Shift + Enter
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Keyboard shortcut to execute the current cell in a SQL notebook.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to quickly run a query without using the mouse.

important_features_or_tools.name: Schedule Button
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Opens the scheduling dialog where you can create a job to run your pipeline automatically on a fixed schedule.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to automate your pipeline so it runs daily (or on a custom schedule) without manual intervention.

important_features_or_tools.name: New Schedule Dialog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A dialog where you configure job scheduling options including job name, frequency, specific run time, and notifications.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When setting up a new scheduled job for the first time.

important_parameters.meaning: Optional name to identify the scheduled job
How often the job runs (default is once per day)
Option to set a specific time for the job to run
Option to configure notifications when the job runs

important_features_or_tools.name: Jobs & Pipelines List
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A page where you can view all your scheduled jobs, see their run history, and manage them.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to monitor job performance, view past runs, or manually trigger a job with the 'Run now' button.

important_features_or_tools.name: Run now Button
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Manually triggers a scheduled job to run immediately instead of waiting for the next scheduled time.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to test a job or refresh your data immediately without waiting for the scheduled time.

practical_workflow.action: In the pipeline asset browser sidebar, click 'Add' then 'Exploration' and create a new SQL notebook with a descriptive name.
practical_workflow.reason: This creates an isolated SQL notebook where you can write queries without affecting your pipeline.

practical_workflow.action: In the SQL notebook, write your first query. Replace `<catalog>.<schema>` with your actual catalog and schema names. For example, query the `top_artists_by_year` table to find artists who released the most songs since 1990.
practical_workflow.reason: Explorations don't use the pipeline's default catalog and schema, so you must specify them explicitly or your query will fail.

practical_workflow.action: Press Shift + Enter to run the query and see the results.
practical_workflow.reason: This executes the query and shows you the data, allowing you to validate your analysis.

practical_workflow.action: Add more queries to additional cells in the same notebook (e.g., a query to find songs with a 4/4 beat and danceable tempo). Replace `<catalog>.<schema>` in each query.
practical_workflow.reason: Organizing related queries in one notebook makes it easy to run multiple analyses together.

practical_workflow.action: Press Shift + Enter to run each new query.
practical_workflow.reason: Each cell can be run independently, so you can test queries one at a time.

practical_workflow.action: Click the 'Schedule' button at the top of the editor to open the scheduling dialog.
practical_workflow.reason: This starts the process of automating your pipeline.

practical_workflow.action: In the 'New schedule' dialog, optionally give the job a name. Accept the default daily schedule or click 'Advanced' to set a specific time.
practical_workflow.reason: Naming helps you identify the job later. Setting a specific time ensures the job runs when you need the data.

practical_workflow.action: Optionally click 'More options' to set up notifications for when the job runs.
practical_workflow.reason: Notifications alert you if the job fails or completes, so you know the status without checking manually.

practical_workflow.action: Click 'Create' to save the schedule and create the job.
practical_workflow.reason: This activates the schedule and your pipeline will now run automatically on the set schedule.

practical_workflow.action: Click 'Schedule' again to view all schedules, or click the job name to go to the 'Jobs & Pipelines' page to monitor runs and view history.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Exploration notebooks do not use the pipeline's default catalog and schema. You must always explicitly specify `<catalog>.<schema>.table_name` in every query, or the query will fail.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that files in the `explorations` folder will run as part of the pipeline.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Files in the `explorations` folder are explicitly excluded from automatic pipeline runs. They are for ad-hoc analysis only. Only pipeline assets run automatically.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming the default daily schedule is the only option.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You can customize the schedule by clicking 'Advanced' to set a specific time, or use 'More options' to add notifications. The default is just a starting point.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not knowing how to run a job immediately for testing.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use the 'Run now' button on the job's page in the 'Jobs & Pipelines' list to trigger the job immediately without waiting for the scheduled time.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, you would create explorations to validate that your ETL pipeline is producing correct results before scheduling it. For example, query the prepared tables to check data quality, row counts, and expected values.
Use multiple cells in one exploration notebook to organize related analyses. For example, one cell for data quality checks, another for business metrics, and another for debugging.

Always remember to replace `<catalog>.<schema>` in exploration queries. A common pattern is to copy the exact catalog and schema names from your pipeline configuration and paste them into every query.

Schedule your pipeline to run at a time when fresh data is available and when you need the results. For example, if you ingest data daily at 2 AM, schedule the pipeline to run at 3 AM so it processes the latest data.
Use the 'Jobs & Pipelines' page to monitor scheduled jobs. Check the run history to ensure jobs are completing successfully and identify any failures that need investigation.
If a scheduled job fails, you can click 'Run now' to test it immediately after making fixes, rather than waiting for the next scheduled run.

This tutorial shows you how to develop and deploy your first ETL (extract, transform, and load) pipeline for data orchestration with Apache Spark. Although this tutorial uses Databricks all-purpose compute, you can also use serverless compute if it's enabled for your workspace.

You can also use Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines to build ETL pipelines. Databricks Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines reduces the complexity of building, deploying, and maintaining production ETL pipelines. See Tutorial: Build an ETL pipeline with Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines.

By the end of this article, you will know how to:

- Launch a Databricks all-purpose compute resource.
- Create a Databricks notebook.
- Configure incremental data ingestion to Delta Lake with Auto Loader.
- Process and interact with data.
- Schedule a notebook as a Databricks job.

This tutorial uses interactive notebooks to complete common ETL tasks in Python or Scala.

You can also use the Databricks Terraform provider to create this article's resources. See Create clusters, notebooks, and jobs with Terraform.

- You are logged into a Databricks workspace.
- You have permission to create a compute resource.

If you do not have compute control privileges, you can still complete most of the steps below as long as you have access to a compute resource.

To do exploratory data analysis and data engineering, create a compute resource to execute commands.

If your workspace is enabled for serverless compute, you can skip this step. Notebooks attach to serverless compute automatically on code execution, or you can select **Serverless** from the compute drop-down. See Serverless compute for notebooks.

- Click  **Compute**in the sidebar.
- On the Compute page, click **Create compute**.
- Specify a unique name for the compute resource, leave the remaining values in their default state, and click **Create compute**.

To learn more about Databricks compute, see Compute.

To create a notebook in your workspace, click  **New** in the sidebar, and then click **Notebook**. A blank notebook opens in the workspace.

To learn more about creating and managing notebooks, see Manage Databricks notebooks.

Databricks recommends using Auto Loader for incremental data ingestion. Auto Loader automatically detects and processes new files as they arrive in cloud object storage.

Databricks recommends storing data with Delta Lake. Delta Lake is an open source storage layer that provides ACID transactions and enables the data lakehouse. Delta Lake is the default format for tables created in Databricks.

To configure Auto Loader to ingest data to a Delta Lake table, copy and paste the following code into the empty cell in your notebook:

- Python
- Scala

```

file_path = "/databricks-datasets/structured-streaming/events"
username = spark.sql("SELECT regexp_replace(session_user(), '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '_')").first()[0]
table_name = f"{username}_etl_quickstart"
checkpoint_path = f"/tmp/{username}/_checkpoint/etl_quickstart"

(spark.readStream
  .format("cloudFiles")
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
  .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", checkpoint_path)
  .load(file_path)
  .select("*", col("_metadata.file_path").alias("source_file"), current_timestamp().alias("processing_time"))
  .writeStream
  .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
  .trigger(availableNow=True)
  .toTable(table_name))
```
```
// Imports
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.current_timestamp
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.Trigger
import spark.implicits._
// Define variables used in code below
val file_path = "/databricks-datasets/structured-streaming/events"
val username = spark.sql("SELECT regexp_replace(session_user(), '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '_')").first.get(0)
val table_name = s"${username}_etl_quickstart"
val checkpoint_path = s"/tmp/${username}/_checkpoint"
// Clear out data from previous demo execution
spark.sql(s"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ${table_name}")
dbutils.fs.rm(checkpoint_path, true)
// Configure Auto Loader to ingest JSON data to a Delta table
spark.readStream
  .format("cloudFiles")
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
  .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", checkpoint_path)
  .load(file_path)
  .select($"*", $"_metadata.file_path".as("source_file"), current_timestamp.as("processing_time"))
  .writeStream
  .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
  .trigger(Trigger.AvailableNow)
  .toTable(table_name)
```
The variables defined in this code should allow you to safely execute it without risk of conflicting with existing workspace assets or other users. Restricted network or storage permissions will raise errors when executing this code; contact your workspace administrator to troubleshoot these restrictions.

To learn more about Auto Loader, see What is Auto Loader?.

reference_note.title: Build Your First ETL Pipeline with Databricks
reference_note.summary: This tutorial teaches you how to create a complete ETL pipeline using Databricks notebooks, compute resources, and Auto Loader for data ingestion into Delta Lake. You'll learn to set up compute, create a notebook, configure incremental data loading, and schedule jobs—all the essentials to start a real Databricks project quickly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: ETL stands for Extract, Transform, and Load. It's a process where you pull data from a source, modify it to be useful, and store it in a destination like Delta Lake.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Most real Databricks projects involve moving and processing data. Understanding ETL helps you structure your data workflows correctly from the start.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A compute resource is a cluster of machines that runs your code. You need to create one before you can execute any commands in notebooks.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Without compute, your notebooks cannot run. You must create or attach to a compute resource to execute any data processing tasks.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: An interactive document where you write and execute code (Python or Scala) cell by cell. It's where you build your ETL logic.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Notebooks are the primary tool for developing and testing ETL pipelines in Databricks. They let you see results immediately and iterate quickly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks feature that automatically detects and processes new files as they arrive in cloud storage. It handles incremental data ingestion for you.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Auto Loader is the recommended way to ingest data incrementally. It saves you from manually checking for new files and avoids reprocessing old data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: An open-source storage layer that stores data in a format that supports ACID transactions (reliable, consistent updates). It's the default table format in Databricks.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Delta Lake ensures your data is reliable and consistent. It's the standard way to store tables in Databricks, so you should use it for all your data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A scheduled or triggered execution of a notebook. Jobs allow you to run your ETL pipeline automatically on a schedule or when certain conditions are met.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In production, you don't want to manually run notebooks. Jobs automate your ETL pipeline so it runs reliably without manual intervention.

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A section in the Databricks sidebar where you create and manage compute resources (clusters) that execute your code.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you first set up Databricks or need to create a new cluster to run notebooks.

important_features_or_tools.name: Create Compute

important_parameters.meaning: A unique identifier for your cluster

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: An interactive document in Databricks where you write and execute code in cells. Supports Python and Scala.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: For developing, testing, and running ETL pipelines. Create a new notebook by clicking New > Notebook in the sidebar.

important_features_or_tools.name: Auto Loader (cloudFiles format)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Spark streaming feature that automatically detects and ingests new files from cloud storage. Configured using spark.readStream with format('cloudFiles').
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to incrementally load new data files as they arrive. This is the recommended approach for data ingestion in Databricks.

important_parameters.meaning: The file format to ingest (e.g., 'json', 'csv', 'parquet')
A path where Auto Loader stores schema information and checkpoint data. Must be a writable location.

important_features_or_tools.name: checkpointLocation
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A path where Spark stores checkpoint data to track which files have been processed. Prevents reprocessing the same files.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always set this when using writeStream. Use the same path as cloudFiles.schemaLocation.

important_parameters.meaning: Path to store checkpoint metadata

important_features_or_tools.name: trigger(availableNow=True) / Trigger.AvailableNow
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Processes all available data once and then stops. Useful for batch processing instead of continuous streaming.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to process data once rather than continuously stream it. Good for scheduled jobs.

important_parameters.meaning: Trigger mode that processes all available data once

important_features_or_tools.name: toTable(table_name)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Writes the processed data to a Delta Lake table with the specified name. Creates the table if it doesn't exist.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: At the end of your ETL pipeline to store the final processed data.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the Delta Lake table to create or write to

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks Job
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A scheduling and orchestration feature that runs notebooks on a schedule or when triggered. Allows you to automate your ETL pipeline.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to run your ETL notebook automatically (e.g., daily, hourly) without manual intervention.

important_features_or_tools.name: Serverless Compute
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: An alternative to all-purpose compute that automatically manages compute resources. Available if enabled in your workspace.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: If your workspace has serverless compute enabled, you can skip manual cluster creation. Notebooks attach to serverless compute automatically.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to run code in a notebook without creating or attaching to a compute resource first.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always create a compute resource (or use serverless compute if available) before executing notebook code. Compute is required to run any commands.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not setting checkpointLocation when using Auto Loader, which causes data to be reprocessed.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always set checkpointLocation in your writeStream options. This tells Spark which files have already been processed, preventing duplicates.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Storing data in formats other than Delta Lake.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use Delta Lake (the default format in Databricks) for all your tables. It provides ACID guarantees and is optimized for Databricks workflows.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Manually running notebooks in production instead of scheduling them as jobs.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use Databricks Jobs to schedule your notebooks. This automates your ETL pipeline and ensures it runs reliably without manual intervention.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing Auto Loader with manual file loading. Auto Loader is for incremental ingestion of new files.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Auto Loader automatically detects new files as they arrive. Use it when you expect new data files to be added over time. For one-time data loads, you can use simpler methods.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, your ETL pipeline will read from cloud storage (S3, Azure Blob Storage, GCS), transform the data using Spark SQL or DataFrame APIs, and write results to Delta Lake tables.
Use the checkpoint_path variable pattern shown in the tutorial to avoid conflicts with other users in shared workspaces. The code uses regexp_replace to sanitize usernames.
Auto Loader with trigger(availableNow=True) is ideal for scheduled batch jobs. For continuous streaming, use trigger(processingTime='5 minutes') or similar.
Always include metadata columns (like source_file and processing_time) in your ingested data. This helps with debugging and auditing in production.
Once your notebook works correctly, schedule it as a Databricks Job to run automatically (e.g., daily). This is how ETL pipelines run in production.
If you encounter permission errors when running the code, contact your workspace administrator. They may need to grant you access to cloud storage or adjust network policies.
For complex ETL pipelines, consider using Databricks Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines as an alternative to reduce complexity.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: In Databricks notebooks, you write code in cells and run them one at a time. Each cell executes independently, and you can see results immediately.

If you're interested in Databricks for your personal use, sign up for Databricks Free Edition by going to the Databricks Free Edition signup page. Choose your preferred signup method, and then Databricks will create a new workspace for you to use.

Free Edition replaced the legacy Databricks Community Edition, which was retired in 2025. If you previously used Community Edition, sign up for Free Edition to continue your work.

Databricks Free Edition is a no-cost version of Databricks designed for students, educators, hobbyists, and anyone interested in learning or experimenting with data and AI.

Free Edition gives you an easy-to-use Databricks workspace where you can explore datasets, build and share projects, and work with AI and machine learning tools. It’s ideal for learning, prototyping, and collaborative exploration.

Databricks Free Edition is available in a serverless-only, quota-limited environment that contains many of the same features included with the full Databricks platform, with some limitations (see Databricks Free Edition limitations). With a Free Edition account, you can do the following:

-
**Build AI applications and agents**: Prepare data, experiment with foundation models, and deploy, evaluate, and govern AI systems.
-
**Collaborate on data science and ML projects**: Use shared notebooks to work with others in real time and publish results for others to review. Ideal for group projects, tutorials, and collaborative experimentation.
-
**Explore and analyze real datasets**: Use the SQL editor or notebooks to build hands-on experience with querying and visualizing real data.
-
**Create interactive dashboards**: Use Genie to interact with and visualize your data using natural-language prompts.
-
**Design and test data pipelines**: Ingest, transform, and orchestrate data across different sources using Lakeflow.
-
**Access Genie Code**: Use Genie Code to get in-product coding help. Genie Code can suggest, explain, and fix code directly within notebooks, queries, and files.
-
**Build a database application**: Use Lakebase Postgres to build real-time transactional applications alongside your lakehouse data.

Your new workspace includes serverless compute and default storage, so you can immediately start exploring and building on Databricks. Use the following tutorials to help get you started:

reference_note.title: Getting Started with Databricks Free Edition
reference_note.summary: Databricks Free Edition is a no-cost workspace for learning and experimenting with data and AI. It replaced Community Edition and gives you immediate access to a serverless environment where you can build AI applications, collaborate on projects, explore datasets, and create dashboards—all without setup costs. Sign up on the Databricks website to get started instantly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A free, no-cost version of Databricks designed for students, hobbyists, and learners. It provides a ready-to-use workspace with serverless compute and storage included, so you can start working immediately without infrastructure setup.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: It removes the barrier to entry for learning Databricks. You can prototype ideas, build real projects, and learn data and AI tools without paying anything or managing servers.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Your personal Databricks environment where you write code, store data, and build projects. When you sign up for Free Edition, Databricks automatically creates one for you.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: The workspace is where all your work lives—notebooks, datasets, dashboards, and AI models. It's your central hub for all Databricks activities.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Computing power that runs automatically when you need it, without you having to create or manage clusters. It's included in Free Edition.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You don't need to worry about setting up or scaling infrastructure. You can focus on your data and code instead of DevOps.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Free Edition has usage limits (like storage, compute time, or API calls) to keep costs down. You won't be charged, but you may hit limits if you use it heavily.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understand that Free Edition is for learning and prototyping, not production workloads. If you outgrow it, you can upgrade to a paid plan.

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to query data quickly without writing Python or Scala code. Ideal for data exploration and analysis.

This page explains how to create your Databricks account and start your free trial. With the free trial, you are eligible to receive credit for free Databricks usage, valid for 14 days after you start your trial.

First, choose the trial that best meets your organization's needs. Both versions include free Databricks usage credits valid for 14 days after you start your trial.

- Express signup: Express setup is a quick way to start using Databricks without requiring prior cloud provider access. You can sign up with an email address and immediately begin using a serverless workspace. You can upgrade your account by adding a payment method or signing a commitment with Databricks. After you upgrade, you can also create a classic workspace with resources deployed in your AWS account.
- Sign up with your existing AWS account: You can also start your free trial through AWS Marketplace. You will automatically receive a serverless workspace and can begin working immediately. You also have the option to create a classic workspace with resources deployed in your AWS account. When your trial ends or you use all your credits, your Databricks account switches to a pay-as-you-go model, with billing managed in your AWS console.

To view your remaining trial credits or upgrade from a trial account, click the **Manage trial** button in the top bar of your workspace.

At any point during your free trial, you can enter your payment information to upgrade your account. Upgrading your account gives you immediate access to the full Databricks platform without trial limitations. Any remaining trial credits will still be available after the upgrade.

If you signed up with express setup, you can add a credit card or link an AWS account if you prefer to be billed through AWS. To switch from monthly credit-card billing to invoice or commit billing, contact a Databricks representative.

If you signed up for the free trial using AWS Marketplace, charges appear on the AWS Billing & Cloud Management dashboard alongside your other AWS charges. After the free trial period, you are billed only for the resources you use.

You can cancel your subscription at any time. If you have signed up for the trial through AWS Marketplace or added a payment method to your Databricks account, your subscription will automatically be converted to a pay-as-you-go account after you exhaust your trial credits. To cancel during the free trial and avoid incurring costs after your trial ends, you must first do the following:

- Terminate all compute resources.
- Remove your credit card information from your account, if applicable.

After completing these steps, you can cancel your subscription. These actions prevent your account from converting to a pay-as-you-go account that accumulates charges. See Cancel your Databricks plan.

:::

Generally, free trial accounts created using personal emails are subject to certain limitations. To avoid trial limitations, sign up using a business email. Possible limitations include:

- Limited scaling of serverless compute resources:
- Maximum one SQL warehouse per workspace that will scale to a maximum of 50 DBUs/hr.
- Serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines will scale to a maximum of 50 DBUs/hr.
- No access to GPUs (CPU only).
- AI Search is limited to one endpoint with a scale capped to 1 search unit.

- Limited external network access. To access a blocked public dataset, Databricks recommends manually downloading the dataset and then uploading it to your workspace. See Work with files in Unity Catalog volumes.
- Generally, trial workspaces include many of the latest Databricks releases, but some features may be limited or unavailable.

reference_note.title: Databricks Free Trial Account Limitations
reference_note.summary: Free trial accounts created with personal emails have resource and feature limitations that can restrict your ability to build and scale projects. Signing up with a business email removes most limitations. Key restrictions include capped compute resources (50 DBUs/hr maximum), no GPU access, limited AI Search, and restricted external network access. Understanding these limits helps you plan your project architecture and decide whether to upgrade.

This 5-minute no-code tutorial introduces generative AI on Databricks. You will use the AI Playground to do the following:

- Query large language models (LLMs) and compare results side-by-side
- Prototype a tool-calling AI agent
- Export your agent to Databricks Apps or to a notebook
- Optional: Prototype a question-answer chatbot using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Ensure your workspace can access the following:

- Unity Catalog.
- Custom Agents. See Features with limited regional availability.

Use the AI Playground to query LLMs in a chat interface.

- In your workspace, select **Playground**from the left navigation pane under**AI/ML**.
- Type a question such as, "What is RAG?"

Add a new LLM to compare responses side-by-side:

- In the upper-right, select **+**to add a model for comparison.
- In the new pane, select a different model using the dropdown selector.
- Select the **Sync**checkboxes to synchronize the queries.
- Try a new prompt, such as, "What is a compound AI system?" to see the two responses side-by-side.

Keep testing and comparing different LLMs to help you decide on the best one to use to build an AI agent.

Tools allow LLMs to do more than generate language. Tools can query external data, run code, and take other actions. AI Playground gives you a no-code option to prototype tool-calling agents:

-
From Playground, choose a model labelled **Tools enabled**.
-
Select **Tools**>**+ Add tool**and select the built-in Unity Catalog function,`system.ai.python_exec`.This function lets your agent run arbitrary Python code. Other tool options include: - **UC Function**: Select a Unity Catalog function for your agent to use.
- **Function definition**: Define a custom function for your agent to call.
- **AI Search**: Specify an AI Search index. If your agent uses an AI Search index, its response will cite the sources used.
- **MCP**: Specify MCP servers to use managed Databricks MCP servers or external MCP servers.

-
Ask a question that involves generating or running Python code. You can try different variations on your prompt phrasing. If you add multiple tools, the LLM selects the appropriate tool to generate a response.

If you have an AI Search index set up in your workspace, you can prototype a question-answer bot. This type of agent uses documents in an AI Search index to answer questions based on those documents.

-
Click **Tools**>**+ Add tool**. Then, select your AI Search index.
-
Ask a question related to your documents. The agent can use the index to look up relevant info and will cite any documents used in its answer.

To set up an AI Search index, see Create an AI Search index.

reference_note.title: Getting Started with Generative AI on Databricks Using AI Playground
reference_note.summary: AI Playground is a no-code interface in Databricks where you can query large language models, compare their responses side-by-side, and prototype AI agents with tools (like Python code execution or document search). You can test different models, add capabilities to your agents, and export working prototypes to notebooks or Databricks Apps without writing code.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A chat-like interface in Databricks where you can ask questions to different AI models and see their responses. It's designed for testing and prototyping without writing code.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: It lets you quickly experiment with different AI models and agent configurations before committing to building a full application, saving time in the planning phase of your project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: AI agents that can do more than just generate text—they can run Python code, query databases, search documents, or call custom functions to answer questions more accurately.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tools extend what your AI agent can do. Instead of just generating text, it can fetch real data, run calculations, or search your documents to provide accurate, grounded answers.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A technique where an AI agent searches through your documents or data to find relevant information, then uses that information to answer your question and cite sources.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: RAG makes AI agents more reliable for your project because answers are based on your actual data rather than the model's training data, and sources are cited so you know where information came from.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks' system for managing data, functions, and resources in your workspace. It's required to use AI Playground.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Unity Catalog is a prerequisite for using AI Playground, and it's where you store the functions and data your AI agents will access.

After testing your agent in AI Playground, export it so that you can deploy, evaluate, and iterate on it outside the Playground. AI Playground offers two export paths:

- **Export to Databricks Apps (recommended)**: Installs a deployable agent app from the- `agent-openai-agents-sdk`template, including a built-in chat UI, MCP tool wiring, and authentication. Choose this path for new agents.
- **Create agent notebook (legacy)**: Generates a Python notebook that defines the agent and deploys it to a Model Serving endpoint. Choose this path if Databricks Apps is not available in your workspace or region.

- Export to Apps (recommended)
- Create agent notebook (legacy)

The **Export to Databricks Apps** option generates a deployed agent app that's ready to chat with. The app uses the same model, system prompt, and tools (including MCP servers and vector search) you configured in the Playground.

Before you export, make sure your workspace meets the following requirements:

- Databricks Apps must be enabled in your workspace. See Set up your Databricks Apps workspace and development environment.
- The endpoint selected in Step 2 must support tools.
- The **Managed MCP Servers**preview must be enabled in your workspace. See Manage Databricks previews.

To export the agent:

-
In the Playground, click **Get code**>**Export to Databricks Apps**.
-
In the **Export to Databricks Apps**dialog, set the following:- **App Name**: A unique name that starts with- `agent-`and contains only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens (for example,- `agent-research-assistant`).
- **App Description**: A short description of what the agent does.
- **MLflow Experiment**: Select an existing MLflow experiment to use for tracing and evaluation, or create a new one.

-
Click **Export**. Databricks does the following:- Validates that the app name is available.
- Installs the `agent-openai-agents-sdk`template into your workspace and grants the app permissions for the resources it needs. These resources include the MLflow experiment, serving endpoint, and any MCP servers, Unity Catalog functions, Genie Agents, or vector search indexes you added as tools.
- Generates `agent_server/agent.py`from your Playground configuration so the deployed agent matches what you tested.

-
When the success dialog appears, click **View Agent**to open the deployed app and chat with it using the built-in UI.

To customize the agent code, configure authentication, add evaluation, or redeploy with Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs), see Author an AI agent and deploy it on Databricks Apps.

After testing your agent in AI Playground, click **Get code** > **Create agent notebook** to export your agent to a Python notebook.

After you export the agent code, Databricks saves a folder with a driver notebook to your workspace. This driver defines a tool-calling ResponsesAgent, tests the agent locally, uses code-based logging, registers, and deploys the AI agent using Custom Agents.

The exported notebook currently uses a legacy agent authoring workflow that deploys the agent to Model Serving. Databricks recommends authoring agents using Databricks Apps instead. See Author an AI agent and deploy it on Databricks Apps.

If you want Databricks to run the agent loop for you, you can use the Supervisor API (Beta) instead of writing your own. The Supervisor API supports Databricks-hosted tools (Unity Catalog functions, Genie Agents, MCP servers) and client-side function tools that execute in your application code. Choose this option when you don't need custom Python logic between tool calls.

To try it from your Playground configuration, make sure you've added at least one tool in Step 2, then click **Get code** > **Curl API**. When the Playground deployment has tools and uses a Supervisor-compatible model, the curl is a Supervisor API `POST` request to `/mlflow/v1/responses` with your model, prompt, and hosted tools. The option also requires the **Supervisor API** preview to be enabled. See Manage Databricks previews.

To deploy a Supervisor API agent on Databricks Apps, see Build a custom agent using the Supervisor API (Beta).

To author agents using a code-first approach, see Author an AI agent and deploy it on Databricks Apps.

Each path has different requirements and use cases depending on your workspace setup and needs.

In this tutorial, you use Genie Code to run end-to-end customer segmentation directly inside a Databricks notebook. Starting from a raw marketing campaign data set, Genie Code handles data profiling, feature engineering, K-means clustering, and persona generation — all from a single prompt.

- A Databricks workspace with Genie Code enabled.
- Partner-powered AI features enabled for both the account and workspace. See Partner-powered AI features.
- Genie Code Agent mode preview enabled. See Manage Databricks previews.

For this tutorial, you use a marketing campaign data set.

- Download the Marketing Campaign data set from Kaggle.
- Click  **New > Add or upload data**.
- Click **Create or modify a table**.
- Click **browse**or drag and drop the downloaded file onto the drop zone.
- Select the target catalog and schema in Unity Catalog.
- (Optional) Edit the table name.
- Click **Create table**.

- In the sidebar, click **New**and select**Notebook**.
- Name the notebook **Marketing Campaign Data**.
- Attach the notebook to compute or use serverless compute.

Genie Code in Agent mode can plan and run multi-step tasks autonomously — it reads cell outputs, fixes errors, and adapts its approach based on results.

- In the upper-right corner of the notebook, click to open the Genie Code pane.
- In the mode selector at the bottom of the Genie Code pane, select **Agent**.

Segmentation analysis is commonly performed by clustering customers who have similar purchase patterns together. For example, segments might be based on income, demographics, or specific purchasing behaviors. One common approach is K-means clustering, a technique that automatically groups similar customers into distinct segments, called "clusters."

Tell Genie Code (Agent mode) to do this for you:

```
Help me cluster my customers from my marketing campaign to profile them. I want to identify interesting segments that may be useful for marketing purposes.
```
Genie Code breaks down the prompt into steps and runs them:

- **Understands context**— Genie Code reads your prompt and the current state of the notebook.
- **Finds relevant data**— Genie Code searches Unity Catalog for relevant data assets and loads them for analysis.
- **Generates and runs code**— Genie Code edits notebook cells following a standard data science workflow: importing libraries, preprocessing data, training the model, and visualizing results.
- **Summarizes results**— Genie Code has a plain-language summary of what it found.

Genie Code asks for your approval before running code. Review each step and click **Allow**. You can also select **Allow in this thread** to approve all steps in the current conversation, or **Always allow** to skip future approval prompts.

After Genie Code finishes, review the generated notebook cells and the summary in the Genie Code pane. The summary describes each identified customer segment, including demographic characteristics, purchase behavior, and suggestions for how to engage each group.

For example, Genie Code might identify segments like **Premium Loyalists** (high-income, frequent buyers) and **Bargain Seekers** (price-sensitive, promotion-driven).

Use follow-up prompts to dig deeper into the analysis:

- `Are there any other clustering techniques we should consider?`
- `What happens if we increase the number of clusters?`
- `Filter to customers who have made a purchase in the last 90 days.`

Each follow-up prompt builds on the previous results without starting over.

reference_note.title: Customer Segmentation with Databricks Genie Code
reference_note.summary: Genie Code is an AI-powered feature in Databricks notebooks that can automatically perform end-to-end data analysis tasks like customer segmentation. You upload your data, create a notebook, enable Genie Code in Agent mode, and describe what you want to analyze in plain language. Genie Code then generates and runs the code for you, handling data profiling, feature engineering, clustering, and result summarization.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: An AI assistant built into Databricks notebooks that can write and run code for you based on plain-language prompts. You describe what analysis you want, and it generates the Python/SQL code, runs it, and explains the results.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you perform complex data analysis without writing code yourself, making it much faster to get insights from your data in a real project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A special mode where Genie Code can plan and execute multi-step tasks on its own. It reads the output of each step, fixes errors if they occur, and adjusts its approach based on what it learns.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Allows Genie Code to handle complex workflows automatically, like the entire customer segmentation pipeline, without you having to run each step manually.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A technique that automatically groups similar customers together into distinct segments (called clusters) based on patterns in their data, like purchase behavior or income.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Helps you identify customer segments for marketing purposes without manually defining what makes customers similar.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks' system for organizing and storing data. When you upload a dataset, you choose which catalog and schema to store it in.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Keeps your data organized and makes it easy for Genie Code to find and access the data you want to analyze.

important_features_or_tools.name: Genie Code Pane
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A panel in the notebook where you write prompts to Genie Code and review its responses, generated code, and analysis summaries.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Open it whenever you want to ask Genie Code to perform analysis or generate code.

important_features_or_tools.name: Agent Mode Selector
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A dropdown at the bottom of the Genie Code pane that lets you switch Genie Code to Agent mode, enabling autonomous multi-step task execution.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Select this when you want Genie Code to handle complex workflows automatically without you running each step individually.

important_features_or_tools.name: New > Add or upload data
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A menu option in the Databricks workspace sidebar that lets you upload a dataset file.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you have a CSV or other data file you want to use in Databricks.

important_features_or_tools.name: Create or modify a table
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: After uploading a file, this option converts the file into a table stored in Unity Catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After uploading your data file, to make it queryable and accessible to notebooks.

important_features_or_tools.name: New > Notebook
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new notebook where you can write code and interact with Genie Code.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When starting a new analysis or project in Databricks.

important_features_or_tools.name: Attach to compute or use serverless compute
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Connects your notebook to computing resources so it can run code. Serverless compute is managed automatically by Databricks.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Required before you can run any code in a notebook.

important_features_or_tools.name: Approval Buttons (Allow, Allow in this thread, Always allow)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Controls whether Genie Code can run the code it generates. 'Allow' approves one step, 'Allow in this thread' approves all steps in the current conversation, 'Always allow' skips future approval prompts.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Review each generated step before approving it to ensure the code does what you expect.

important_features_or_tools.name: Follow-up Prompts
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Additional plain-language requests you can make to Genie Code after the initial analysis. Each builds on previous results without restarting.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to explore different aspects of your data or try alternative approaches (e.g., 'What if we increase the number of clusters?').

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to write all the code yourself to use Databricks.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Genie Code can write and run the code for you based on plain-language prompts. You describe what you want, and it handles the implementation.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Uploading a file and expecting Genie Code to find it automatically without creating a table.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You must convert your uploaded file into a table in Unity Catalog. Genie Code searches Unity Catalog for data, not loose files.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking Agent mode means Genie Code will run code without your approval.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Agent mode means Genie Code can plan and execute multi-step tasks autonomously, but it still asks for your approval before running code. You can approve individual steps or all steps in a conversation.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming each follow-up prompt starts the analysis from scratch.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Follow-up prompts build on previous results. Genie Code remembers what it has already done and uses that context for new requests.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, you would start by uploading your actual customer or marketing data to Databricks, creating a table in Unity Catalog, and then using Genie Code to automatically perform segmentation analysis without writing code.
Genie Code handles the entire data science workflow (data profiling, feature engineering, model training, visualization) in one go, saving significant time compared to writing each step manually.
The generated segments (e.g., 'Premium Loyalists', 'Bargain Seekers') provide actionable insights you can use immediately for marketing campaigns or business decisions.
Use follow-up prompts to experiment with different clustering approaches or parameters (e.g., different numbers of clusters) to find the segmentation that best fits your business needs.
Review the generated notebook cells to understand what Genie Code did. This helps you learn the underlying data science techniques and modify the analysis if needed in future projects.

This tutorial walks you through using a Databricks notebook to import data from a CSV file containing baby name data from health.data.ny.gov into your Unity Catalog volume using Python, Scala, and R. You also learn to modify a column name, visualize the data, and save to a table.

If you are using Databricks Free Edition, select the **Python** tab for all code examples in this tutorial. Free Edition does not support R or Scala. Additionally, Free Edition restricts outbound internet access, so you must upload the CSV file using the workspace UI instead of downloading it with code. See Step 3 for detailed instructions.

To complete the tasks in this article, you must meet the following requirements:

- Your workspace must have Unity Catalog enabled. For information on getting started with Unity Catalog, see Get started with Unity Catalog. Databricks Free Edition and free trial workspaces have Unity Catalog enabled by default.
- You must have the `WRITE VOLUME`privilege on a volume, the`USE SCHEMA`privilege on the parent schema, and the`USE CATALOG`privilege on the parent catalog. Free Edition users have these privileges on the workspace catalog and`default`schema by default.
- You must have permission to use an existing compute resource or create a new compute resource. See Compute or see your Databricks administrator.

For a completed notebook for this article, see Import and visualize data notebooks.

To create a notebook in your workspace, click  **New** in the sidebar, and then click **Notebook**. A blank notebook opens in the workspace.

To learn more about creating and managing notebooks, see Manage Databricks notebooks.

In this step, you define variables for use in the example notebook you create in this article. You need the names of a Unity Catalog catalog, schema, and volume.

If you don't know your catalog and schema names, click  **Catalog** in the sidebar. The workspace catalog shares a name with your workspace and is listed in the catalog panel. Expand it to see available schemas. Free Edition and free trial users can use the workspace catalog and the `default` schema.

If you don't have a volume, create one by running the following command in a notebook cell (replace `<catalog_name>` and `<schema_name>` with your values):

```
CREATE VOLUME IF NOT EXISTS <catalog_name>.<schema_name>.my_volume
```
-
Copy and paste the following code into the new empty notebook cell. Replace `<catalog-name>`,`<schema-name>`, and`<volume-name>`with the catalog, schema, and volume names for a Unity Catalog volume. Optionally replace the`table_name`value with a table name of your choice. You save the baby name data into this table later in this article.
-
Press `Shift+Enter`to run the cell and create a new blank cell.- Python
- Scala
- R

 schema = "<schema_name>"
 volume = "<volume_name>"
 download_url = "https://health.data.ny.gov/api/views/jxy9-yhdk/rows.csv"
 file_name = "baby_names.csv"
 table_name = "baby_names"
 path_volume = "/Volumes/" + catalog + "/" + schema + "/" + volume
 path_table = catalog + "." + schema
 print(path_table) # Show the complete path

 val volume = "<volume_name>"

 val fileName = "baby_names.csv"

 val pathVolume = s"/Volumes/${catalog}/${schema}/${volume}"
 val pathTable = s"${catalog}.${schema}"

reference_note.title: Import CSV Data into Databricks Unity Catalog Volume
reference_note.summary: This tutorial teaches you how to set up a Databricks notebook to import CSV data into a Unity Catalog volume, then visualize and save it as a table. You'll define variables for your catalog, schema, and volume, then use them to build file paths for data storage. The tutorial supports Python, Scala, and R, but Free Edition users must use Python and upload files manually.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A centralized system in Databricks that organizes and manages data access. It has three levels: catalogs (top level), schemas (middle level), and volumes or tables (bottom level).

reference_note.title: Saving DataFrames to Unity Catalog Tables
reference_note.summary: To save a DataFrame to Unity Catalog, you need CREATE table privileges on the catalog and schema. You must rename columns with special characters (like spaces) using withColumnRenamed(), then save the DataFrame as a table using saveAsTable() with overwrite mode. Finally, verify the table was created using the Catalog Explorer UI.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Unity Catalog controls who can do what with data. To save a table, you need CREATE privileges on both the catalog (top-level container) and the schema (folder inside the catalog).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Without the right permissions, your code will fail when trying to save data. You need to ensure your Databricks account has these permissions before starting a project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks column names cannot contain special characters like spaces. You must rename columns before saving the DataFrame.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If your source data has spaces in column names, your save operation will fail. This is a common issue when loading data from external sources.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Write mode controls what happens if a table already exists. 'overwrite' mode replaces the entire table with new data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you often need to refresh tables with new data. Understanding write modes prevents accidental data loss or conflicts.

important_features_or_tools.name: withColumnRenamed()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Renames a column in a DataFrame. Takes the old column name and new column name as parameters.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When your DataFrame has column names with spaces or special characters that are not allowed in Databricks tables.

important_parameters.meaning: The current name of the column you want to rename
The new name for the column (must not contain spaces or special characters)

important_features_or_tools.name: saveAsTable()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Saves a DataFrame as a table in Unity Catalog. Takes a fully qualified table name (catalog.schema.table) as a parameter.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to persist a DataFrame as a permanent table that can be queried later and shared across notebooks.

important_parameters.meaning: The fully qualified table name in format: catalog_name.schema_name.table_name
What to do if the table already exists. 'overwrite' replaces the entire table.

important_features_or_tools.name: write.mode()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies the write mode before saving. Must be chained with saveAsTable().
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Every time you save a DataFrame to control whether you replace existing data or handle conflicts.

important_parameters.meaning: The write behavior: 'overwrite' replaces the table completely

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A visual interface in Databricks that lets you browse catalogs, schemas, and tables. Accessible from the left sidebar.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After saving a table, to verify it was created successfully and to inspect its schema and sample data.

important_features_or_tools.name: Overview tab
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Shows the table schema (column names and data types) when you click on a table in Catalog Explorer.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: To verify that your column names were renamed correctly and that data types are as expected.

important_features_or_tools.name: Sample Data tab
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Displays the first 100 rows of data from a table in Catalog Explorer.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: To quickly inspect the actual data in your table and verify the save operation worked correctly.

practical_workflow.action: Check that you have CREATE privileges on your target catalog and schema in Unity Catalog
practical_workflow.reason: Without these permissions, the save operation will fail. Verify this before writing code.

practical_workflow.action: Identify any columns in your DataFrame with spaces or special characters
practical_workflow.reason: Databricks does not allow these characters in column names, so they must be renamed before saving.

practical_workflow.action: Use withColumnRenamed() to rename problematic columns, replacing spaces with underscores
practical_workflow.reason: This prepares your DataFrame for saving by making all column names valid.

practical_workflow.action: Chain write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable() with your fully qualified table name (catalog.schema.table)
practical_workflow.reason: This saves the DataFrame as a permanent table in Unity Catalog that persists across sessions.

practical_workflow.action: Open Catalog Explorer from the left sidebar and navigate to your catalog and schema
practical_workflow.reason: This verifies that the table was created successfully.

practical_workflow.action: Click on your table and check the Overview tab to see the schema
practical_workflow.reason: Confirms that column names are correct and data types are as expected.

practical_workflow.action: Click the Sample Data tab to view 100 rows
practical_workflow.reason: Verifies that the data was saved correctly and is accessible.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to save a DataFrame with column names containing spaces without renaming them first
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use withColumnRenamed() to replace spaces with underscores or other valid characters before calling saveAsTable().

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to assign the result of withColumnRenamed() to a variable (especially in Scala)
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: In Scala, withColumnRenamed() returns a new DataFrame. You must assign it to a variable: val dfRenamedColumn = df.withColumnRenamed(...). In Python, you can reassign to the same variable: df = df.withColumnRenamed(...).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using a table name without the full catalog.schema.table path
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always provide the fully qualified name: catalog_name.schema_name.table_name. This tells Databricks exactly where to save the table.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not checking permissions before attempting to save
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Verify you have CREATE privileges on both the catalog and schema. If you don't, ask your Databricks administrator to grant these permissions.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, you'll often load data from external sources (CSV, JSON, databases) that have column names with spaces. Always rename these columns before saving to Unity Catalog.
Use overwrite mode when you're refreshing a table with new data. Be careful with this mode in production—it deletes all existing data.
After saving a table, use Catalog Explorer to verify the save succeeded. This is a quick sanity check before moving to the next step in your pipeline.
The fully qualified table name (catalog.schema.table) is how you reference tables across Databricks. Use this same format when querying the table in SQL or other notebooks.
For larger projects, consider learning about ETL pipelines (mentioned in the content) to automate the process of loading, transforming, and saving data.

reference_note.summary: This tutorial teaches you how to build a machine learning classification model on Databricks using pre-installed libraries like scikit-learn and MLflow. You'll learn to train a model to predict wine quality, track experiments with MLflow, tune hyperparameters with Optuna, save models to Unity Catalog, and deploy them. The entire workflow uses Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning, which comes with all necessary libraries pre-installed.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A pre-configured environment that comes with machine learning libraries already installed, including scikit-learn, MLflow, and Optuna. You don't need to install these yourself.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Saves setup time and ensures all team members use the same library versions, reducing compatibility issues in real projects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A tool that tracks and manages your machine learning experiments. It records parameters, metrics, and models so you can compare different training runs and reproduce results.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you need to track which model version performed best and what parameters were used. MLflow automates this.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A centralized place to store and manage data, models, and other assets. It provides access control so you can share resources securely with your team.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In production projects, you need to version models, control who can access them, and ensure data governance. Unity Catalog handles this.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The process of automatically testing different settings (hyperparameters) for your model to find the combination that gives the best performance.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Manual tuning is slow and error-prone. Optuna automates this to improve model accuracy without manual trial-and-error.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A machine learning model that predicts categories (in this case, whether wine is 'high-quality' or not) based on input features like alcohol content and acidity.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Classification is one of the most common machine learning tasks. Understanding this workflow applies to many real-world problems.

reference_note.title: MLflow Model Training, Tracking, and Deployment in Databricks
reference_note.summary: MLflow automatically logs your model training runs, metrics, and parameters. You can use Optuna for hyperparameter tuning, search for your best model using MLflow's API, and deploy it as a serving endpoint. This workflow lets you organize experiments, compare results, and put models into production quickly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you call mlflow.sklearn.autolog(), Databricks automatically records your model, metrics, and parameters during training without you writing extra logging code.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Saves time and ensures consistent tracking of all experiments so you can compare models later

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A single training execution. You wrap your training code in mlflow.start_run() to create a tracked experiment record.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Each run is a separate record you can view, compare, and retrieve later to understand what worked best

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Optuna is a library that automatically tests different parameter combinations to find the best model settings. Each trial is logged as a nested MLflow run.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Finds optimal model parameters faster than manual testing, and all results are tracked for comparison

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A way to query all your logged runs and find the best one based on metrics like test accuracy or AUC score.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you programmatically identify your best model without manually checking the UI

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A deployed model that runs on Databricks infrastructure and accepts prediction requests from applications.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Turns your trained model into a live service that other applications can call for predictions

common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always call mlflow.sklearn.autolog() once at the start of your notebook before training any models

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not wrapping training code in mlflow.start_run(), so runs are not organized separately
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use with mlflow.start_run(run_name='descriptive_name'): to create a new tracked run for each training session

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to access model parameters or metrics directly from the model object instead of from MLflow
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use mlflow.search_runs() to retrieve logged metrics and parameters from your runs

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing nested runs with parent runs when using Optuna
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Set nested=True in mlflow.start_run() for each hyperparameter trial so they appear as child runs under a parent experiment

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to deploy a model without saving it to Unity Catalog first
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Save your model to Unity Catalog before using the Serving UI to create an endpoint

project_usage_notes: In a real project, use mlflow.sklearn.autolog() + mlflow.start_run() to track every model you train so you have a complete history of experiments
Use Optuna for hyperparameter tuning when you have time constraints—it scales across multiple machines and all results are tracked in MLflow
Use mlflow.search_runs() to programmatically find your best model instead of manually checking the UI, especially when running many experiments
Always load your best model with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model() before deploying to verify it works correctly on test data
Deploy to a serving endpoint only after you've validated the model's performance and saved it to Unity Catalog—this makes it available as a live API for your application
Use the traffic percentage parameter when deploying to gradually roll out new model versions (e.g., 10% traffic to a new version while keeping 90% on the old one)
Monitor the endpoint state in the Serving UI—it will show 'Not Ready' while deploying and 'Ready' when it's live and accepting requests

reference_note.title: Query Sample Data and Create Visualizations in Databricks Notebooks
reference_note.summary: Learn how to create a Databricks notebook, query sample data from Unity Catalog using SQL, Python, Scala, or R, and visualize the results with charts. This tutorial shows you how to query the samples.nyctaxi.trips table and create a bar chart showing average fare amounts grouped by pickup zip code in just a few steps.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A web-based workspace where you can write and run code in multiple languages (SQL, Python, Scala, R) and see results immediately. Each notebook contains cells that you execute one at a time.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Notebooks are the primary way you interact with Databricks to query data, transform it, and visualize results all in one place.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A centralized system in Databricks that stores and organizes your data. It includes sample datasets like samples.nyctaxi.trips that you can query immediately.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Unity Catalog must be enabled in your workspace to access data. It provides a consistent way to reference tables across your organization.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Pre-loaded example data included in Databricks (like the NYC taxi trips data) that you can query without needing to load your own data first.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Sample datasets let you start learning and testing immediately without waiting for data ingestion, making it faster to get hands-on experience.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Charts and graphs (like bar charts) that you can create directly in notebooks to display query results in a visual format instead of raw tables.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Visualizations help you understand data patterns quickly and communicate findings to others in your project.
